#790. Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response

Children who consume more ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may have stronger brain responses to tempting foods, potentially helping explain why these products are associated with weight gain. A new study published in JAMA Network Open found that children who ate more of these foods showed heightened activity in the brain's reward system when looking at pictures of appetizing foods. Those stronger responses were also associated with increases in body fat over the following year.

Ultra-processed foods include many everyday products, such as breakfast cereals, packaged bread, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and able to remain fresh for extended periods. Many contain artificial sweeteners, coloring agents, and other ingredients rarely used in home cooking. These products make up a substantial portion of children's diets, accounting for approximately 67% of the calories consumed by children in the United States.

Previous research has associated ultra-processed food consumption with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. However, scientists are still trying to understand the biological processes that might explain these connections. The new investigation, supported in part by the National Institutes of Health, combined magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), dietary assessments, and measurements of children's body composition to explore whether the brain's response to food could play a role.

"Children's brains are still developing, habits are still forming and food preferences are still being made. It's an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment," said the study's senior author, Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. "We're particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference."

Brain Scans Reveal a Link to Future Weight Gain

To investigate these connections, the research team studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the ongoing BrainChild study, which examines factors contributing to diabetes and obesity. Every participant had a healthy weight when the research began, giving scientists an opportunity to investigate potential warning signs before excess weight developed.

The brain scans revealed a notable pattern. Children who consumed larger amounts of ultra-processed foods showed greater activity in the dorsal striatum when viewing food pictures. This part of the brain helps regulate reward and motivation, making it particularly relevant to how people respond to desirable foods.

Importantly, children with stronger responses in this brain region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the next year. The findings suggest that heightened sensitivity to food cues may be one factor connecting ultra-processed diets with subsequent weight gain.

How Brain Reward Activity May Influence Body Fat

By the end of the study, children who consumed more ultra-processed foods generally had higher BMI, greater body fat percentage, and larger waist circumference.

The researchers then examined whether differences in brain activity could help account for these associations. When they adjusted their analysis to consider the children's responses in the dorsal striatum, the relationship between ultra-processed food intake and BMI became 31% weaker. The corresponding association with body fat percentage decreased by 44%.

These reductions suggest that the brain's reward response may help explain part of the relationship between ultra-processed food consumption and changes in body composition. Although the results do not demonstrate that these foods directly alter brain function, they provide a possible biological explanation for an association that has been observed in previous research.

"This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain," Page said. "It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time."

The researchers caution that improving children's diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed products are often inexpensive, widely available, and easy to prepare, making them practical choices for households facing financial or time constraints.

"Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution," Page said.

There are also important limitations to consider. Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether eating ultra-processed foods directly causes heightened brain activity or increases in body weight. The findings establish relationships between these factors, but additional research is needed to determine whether one causes another.

Page hopes to address that question in a future intervention study. The proposed research would provide children who regularly consume ultra-processed foods with more minimally processed alternatives. Scientists could then examine whether changing their diets affects how their brains respond to food images and whether any differences are associated with reduced weight gain.

Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue tracking participants as they move through puberty and into early adulthood. By monitoring brain development, body composition, dietary patterns, and general health over time, researchers hope to gain a clearer picture of how childhood nutrition may influence long-term health.

The study was led by Page alongside Jasmin M. Alves, Ella Morgan, Brendan Angelo, Kianna Le, and Jared Smith from the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes, Department of Medicine, and Diabetes and Obesity Research Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California. Additional contributors included Kay Jann of the USC Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California, and Ting Chow and Anny H. Xiang of the Department of Research and Evaluation at Kaiser Permanente Southern California in Pasadena, California.

Funding came from an American Diabetes Association Pathway Accelerator Award [1-14-ACE-36] and the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) [R01DK116858, R01DK134079]. Support for the REDCap database used in the research was provided by the Southern California Clinical and Translational Science Institute [NIH UL1TR001855].

Materials provided by Keck School of Medicine of USC. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#789. Is Halloween About To Become the New Christmas on the Hot 100?

This week's Five Burning Questions looks at new Oct. 31-boosted chart peaks for Michael Jackson's "Thriller" and Tame Impala & JENNIE's "Dracula."

On this week’s Billboard Hot 100 (dated Nov. 14), Halloween comes closer than ever to boosting a spooky-season anthem to the top of its rankings.

Though Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” reigns for a 27th week on the listing, a pair of fright-night favorites — one classic and one new — appear right below it, in Michael Jackson‘s “Thriller” and Tame Impala and JENNIE‘s “Dracula,” respectively. Both hit new peaks this week, and lead the six total Halloween-themed titles on this week’s chart, including one first-time entry: “Spooky, Scary Skeletons,” from late ’70s hitmaker Andrew Gold.

Will “Thriller” get to No. 1 one of these years? And will Halloween someday have close to the same annual impact on the Hot 100 as Christmas does? Billboard staffers answer these questions and more below.

Katie Atkinson: It sure looks like it! And the chart tracking week will allow for even more Halloween music action in the coming years, because Halloween was on a Saturday this year, meaning the only Halloweekend activity was Friday through early Sunday. Next year, it falls on a Sunday, allowing for an extra tracking day, and it just goes up from there. With music streaming at an all-time high, the more closely we can follow people’s listening habits, the more these seasonal spikes will occur.

Kyle Denis: I think we just might be! Obviously, not every Halloween will coincide with a $1 billion-grossing Michael Jackson biopic and a hit single that just so happens to share a name with one of the holiday’s most enduring characters, but 2026 certainly helped refine the sub-genre of “Halloween pop.”

Chris Eggertsen: I hope so! Halloween is my favorite holiday, and I’d love to see an influx of songs about ghosts and monsters flood the Hot 100 starting every late September or so. While it does seem we’re moving in that direction, I don’t think it’ll ever quite match the power of Christmas — a holiday in which seasonal music is so deeply embedded — in terms of Billboard chart dominance.

Lyndsey Havens: I think so and I hope so. Halloween may not be as cheery as Christmas, but it is a bit more inclusive and playfully spooky — and that’s something worth getting behind.Andrew Unterberger: I don’t know if we’re ever going to quite get to the regular 40-of-the-top-50 levels of domination Christmas can now claim at its yearly Hot 100 peak — there are still only a half-dozen Halloween-themed titles on this week’s chart, after all. But yes, failing some major shift in listener trends (or how Billboard measures them), it should become more and more of a factor year over year, as the streaming sea level among contemporary hits continues to lower and seasonal perennials continue to stick out like they do.

Katie Atkinson: Yes, “Thriller” is the obvious contender for the perennial Mariah slot. That being said, I think it’s worth remembering that in addition to Halloween, the MJ catalog has been seeing a boost all year thanks to April’s Michael biopic. So I do wonder if that increased popularity factored into the song reaching its No. 2 peak this year. I love seeing Christmas songs climb up the chart every year, and this will be a new fun holiday race to watch — and could even lead to a song like “Thriller” that many people might assume was already a Hot 100 No. 1 hit possibly taking a four-decade-plus route to getting there.

Kyle Denis: I’m going with yes. Chart watchers will remember that “All I Want for Christmas Is You” didn’t hit No. 1 during its first few holiday-induced reentries. Between “Thriller” playing in a far less crowded field in terms of yearly Halloween-themed releases and a new generation of listeners who are freshly enamored with the King of Pop, I can definitely see the song becoming an every-year No. 1, barring a gargantuan competitor like “Choosin’ Texas.”

Chris Eggertsen: Given its fairly steady upward trajectory over the last close to a decade — from lingering just within or just outside the top 40 starting at the end of the 2010s before hitting No. 2 this year —  it certainly does feel like “Thriller” is destined to hit No. 1, though I do wonder how much of the bump this year was due to the release of the smash-hit Michael biopic. Then again, with a Michael sequel in development and MJ’s music seemingly hotter than it’s been in decades, a No. 1 placement is certainly plausible over the next couple of years. I don’t think we’re necessarily looking at a perennial Halloween No. 1 a la “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” though, as “Thriller” doesn’t (yet) feel quite as undeniable as the Mariah classic, which effectively occupies its own airspace in the canon of Christmas songs.

Lyndsey Havens: It sure could. Obviously, this year, the film Michael helped the superstar enjoy sustained bumps across his catalog. So, I do think “Thriller” had a leg up compared to years prior, but that’s not to say it won’t continue for years to come. All it may need to jump to that top spot next year is a thoughtfully strategic campaign to say “it’s tiiiiime” a la Mariah.

Andrew Unterberger: Yeah, it seems inevitable — maybe even next year, when Halloween falls on a Sunday, meaning “Thriller” should get pretty major streaming numbers throughout that entire weekend. But if not next year then someday. Maybe for the 20th anniversary of MJ’s death in 2029, or the Thriller album’s 50th anniversary in 2032.

Katie Atkinson: This one is trickier. (Trick-or-treatier?) I could see it getting an annual bump, but I think No. 3 will be the highest it climbs on the Hot 100. Think of it as the new “Disturbia” or “The Dead Dance” or “Heads Will Roll” — the kind of modern song that is seasonally appropriate and gets playlisted on all the Halloween party soundtracks, but not to a “Thriller” level.

Kyle Denis: I think it remains in the canon, albeit on the more contemporary side, with cuts like Lady Gaga’s “The Dead Dance”; if Kevin Parker’s goal was to deliver the new-school Halloween anthem, he timed the whole thing pretty perfectly! I’ll admit, I’d be a bit surprised not to see “Dracula” post substantial streaming gains next Halloween.

Chris Eggertsen: “Dracula” is only a year old at this point, so it’s a little too early to tell. Can a song that’s only tangentially “spooky” sink its teeth into the Hot 100 every year in the way more straightforward scary-season tracks like “Thriller,” “Monster Mash” and “Ghostbusters” have managed? I’m not convinced of that yet, but a No. 3 placement also can’t be discounted.

Lyndsey Havens: I think it will have to prove itself. As much as I love the song, it’s been a bit of a sleeper hit since JENNIE hopped on the remix in February, which is to say, the song was already becoming a slow but lasting hit well before Halloween. I think the holiday gave it that final boost, of course, but I’m not sure if it’s a repeatable process or timeline for years to come.

Andrew Unterberger: I think it’ll hang around, but it’ll have some work to do before it can really compete with the Halloween heavy-hitters. Even at its new daily streaming peak on Oct. 31, it was still multiple millions behind any of the other spooky songs on the Hot 100 this week — and may be even further back next year as it fades as a contemporary hit. But with this early moment under its belt, cementing it as a Halloween staple so early in its lifespan, it’s in the best position to eventually join the all-time canon of any song of the last decade or two.

Katie Atkinson: As a parent to children under 10, welcome to the “Spooky, Scary Skeletons” party, everyone else! I’ve been a proud annual listener for the better part of a decade, and I think this is a delightful addition to the Halloween Hot 100 hits. The long and winding path of this song is fascinating, too, between Gold releasing it in the ’90s and then it getting an EDM remix that brought it new life in 2013. Add to that the lore of Gold’s previous career as an easy-listening hitmaker AND that he wrote the flipping Golden Girls theme song and this man had one of the most unpredictable career paths of all time. (Sadly, Gold passed in 2011, so he never saw his song’s EDM-fueled online resurgence.)

Kyle Denis: Honestly, the remixed version of “Spooky, Scary Skeletons” goes off during a daytime Halloween party, so I won’t scoff at it being added to the canon.

Chris Eggertsen: On the one hand, I appreciate the over-the-top Halloween energy Gold brings to “Spooky, Scary Skeletons,” which also weirdly feels engineered for TikTok virality even though it was released in 1996. But unlike “Thriller” or “Monster Mash,” it’s not exactly a bop — IMO, the vibe is more “pre-trick or treat vibe-setter for the kiddos” than “all-ages Halloween party standard.” I won’t be mad if it becomes an annual entry on the Hot 100, but personally, I can take it or leave it.

Lyndsey Havens: Yes! I think (almost) every Halloween song ever made is a worthy addition to the Halloween canon, and surely this one is. It’s perfectly aged and fun and boasts an alliterative title, what more could you want? As we’ve seen with non-holiday hits, the power of TikTok cannot be ignored when it comes to reviving music and trends from an early or even pre-social media era, so I think it’s expected and fun that a Halloween song would benefit from that, too.

Andrew Unterberger: “Skeletons” has clearly hooked the next generation, so it seems like it should only become more of a Halloween fixture from here. Now we just have to figure out additional holidays to attach “Lonely Boy” and “Thank You for Being a Friend” to.

Katie Atkinson: I’m so glad you asked this question so I can write about my favorite offbeat Halloween song of all time! Please do yourselves a favor and listen to “Halloween Spooks” by jazz trio Lambert, Hendricks & Ross. It was a running gag on KROQ’s The Kevin & Bean Show here in Los Angeles (RIP) that Bean would play this song every spooky season just to annoy Kevin, but while it was a joke on the show, I legitimately love it. And now I’m playing it every year around the house to annoy my kids instead.

Kyle Denis: It’s a six-minute, two-part song that’s not really radio-friendly at all, but Beyoncé’s “Haunted” is one of my favorite creepy, spooky, Halloween-adjacent pop joints from the past 15 years.

Chris Eggertsen: I hold a special place in my dark heart for Blue Oyster Cult’s “(Don’t Fear) The Reaper,” which is featured in John Carpenter’s original Halloween — the best Halloween movie of all time and one of my personal favorite films ever. In my mind, the song and the film are inextricably linked, and no other track puts me in the Halloween spirit more than that one. #787. Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them

Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative way to turn a chemical produced by cancer cells into a weapon against them. Instead of delivering toxic drugs throughout the body, their experimental approach uses carbon monoxide released by cancer cells to manufacture anticancer compounds directly inside the cells themselves.

The research, led by Katsunori Tanaka at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI) in Japan, was published in Nature Communications. In laboratory experiments, the team demonstrated that a specially designed compound could trigger drug production inside cancer cells without generating the same toxic substances in healthy cells. Although the technique is still at an early stage, it could eventually provide a way to attack tumors while reducing the harmful side effects associated with conventional cancer treatments.

Turning Cancer's Own Toxic Gas Against It

One of the greatest challenges in cancer treatment is destroying malignant cells without damaging healthy tissue. Traditional chemotherapy can cause serious side effects because its toxic effects are not always limited to tumors. Tanaka and other researchers are investigating more selective strategies that could make cancer treatments safer.

Their long-term goal is to replace the direct delivery of toxic drugs with relatively harmless compounds that become active only after entering cancer cells. These compounds would use substances already present inside tumors to generate therapeutic drugs exactly where they are needed.

Carbon monoxide offers an intriguing opportunity for this approach. Although best known as a poisonous gas produced by sources such as gasoline engines, carbon monoxide is also generated naturally by many types of cancer cells. Because tumors can produce unusually high amounts of the gas, it may serve as a useful biological marker for identifying cancer cells, provided it can be detected.

Scientists in RIKEN's Biofunctional Synthetic Chemistry Laboratory investigated whether they could exploit this difference. Their strategy involved delivering a metal catalyst into cells and using the excess carbon monoxide in cancer cells to drive a chemical reaction that produces a toxic compound. In principle, the reaction would occur primarily in cancer cells, where enough carbon monoxide is available, while sparing normal cells.

Protecting the Catalyst Inside Cancer Cells

To make the system work, the researchers turned to a class of compounds known as palladacycles. These metal-containing compounds can react with carbon monoxide to produce an organic molecule called phenanthridinone. Certain derivatives of phenanthridinone are toxic to cells and have already been incorporated into anticancer drugs.

However, there was a major obstacle. When palladacycles are introduced directly into cells, substances such as glutathione rapidly deactivate their central palladium catalyst. Without an active catalyst, the reaction cannot produce the desired drug.

Tanaka's team addressed this problem by building on its previous work using metal catalysts to carry out chemical reactions in living systems. The researchers enclosed a palladacycle within albumin, a protein commonly found in blood. This protective protein carrier allows the complex to travel through the bloodstream while shielding the palladium catalyst from substances that would otherwise deactivate it after entering cells.

Laboratory Tests Reveal Selective Drug Production

The scientists evaluated their system through a series of experiments. They began by testing different palladacycles to identify which one could generate the greatest amount of phenanthridinone.

Next, they exposed cultured human liver, cervical, breast, and lung cancer cells to the albumin and palladacycle complex for 48 hours. They also tested the compound on a noncancerous cell line to determine whether the same chemical reaction would occur in healthy cells.

After 48 hours, the researchers detected phenanthridinone in the cancer cell lines but not in the normal cells. The findings indicated that the albumin carrier successfully protected the catalyst from glutathione and that the chemical reaction occurred selectively in the cancer cells under the conditions tested.

The team then refined the system so that the newly formed compound could separate from the carrier and move freely throughout the cell. Additional modifications allowed the reaction to generate a particularly toxic phenanthridinone derivative already used in anticancer drugs.

When the researchers introduced this modified system into cultured liver cancer cells, they observed the anticancer compound forming inside the cells. The cells subsequently showed signs of damage caused by the toxic drug, providing proof that the approach could generate a cancer-fighting substance directly within its intended target.

Why the Experimental Drug Did Not Form in Blood

An important safety concern involved carbon monoxide already present in the bloodstream. If that gas triggered the chemical reaction before the compound reached cancer cells, the resulting drug could damage blood cells instead of its intended target.

Fortunately, laboratory testing showed that the toxic drug was not produced in blood. The researchers believe this is because carbon monoxide in the bloodstream is largely attached to hemoglobin, the protein responsible for transporting oxygen. In this bound form, the gas appears to be unavailable for the reaction needed to manufacture the drug.

The finding suggests that the system may be able to travel through blood without prematurely generating harmful substances, although further studies will be needed to establish its safety in living organisms.

"This work represents an important advance in therapeutic in vivo synthetic chemistry," says Tanaka. "In our therapeutic strategy, molecules naturally present or generated within the body -- including disease-associated metabolites -- are used as endogenous chemical feedstocks to synthesize therapeutic molecules directly at the site of disease."

The researchers now plan to move beyond cultured cells and test the approach in animal models. If future experiments are successful, the technology could help establish a new class of cancer treatments that exploit the chemistry of tumors to produce drugs directly at the disease site, potentially limiting damage to healthy tissue.

Starfish Space's first Otter has died, just a month after it reached the final frontier.

The Seattle startup announced on Tuesday (Nov. 3) that its Otter 24C satellite suffered a glitch in low Earth orbit (LEO) and is not recoverable.

The anomaly killed an ambitious mission in the cradle, as Otter 24C was still in the commissioning phase.

Otter 24C launched Oct. 1 on SpaceX's Transporter-18 mission, a rideshare flight that carried a total of 130 payloads to LEO (including a prototype satellite for Project Suncatcher, Google's planned AI constellation).

The Starfish satellite was flying a mission for NASA called Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability, or SSPICY for short. The goal was to "demonstrate technologies necessary for future debris-removal missions as well as for future applications in the servicing and inspection of active spacecraft," according to NASA's SSPICY site.

"This advances NASA's in-space manufacturing and assembly (ISAM) goals to ensure a sustainable space operating environment and builds towards a future where objects can be assembled, repaired and maintained in space, significantly expanding possibilities for science and human exploration," the agency added.

Starfish Space was a natural partner. The Seattle company plans to become a big player in the nascent field of satellite servicing, using its line of Otter craft to repair, refuel or deorbit other satellites for a variety of customers.

SSPICY marked Otter's spaceflight debut. The mission plan called for the 739-pound (335-kilogram) Otter 24C spacecraft to approach and inspect "up to four inoperable space objects of U.S. origin" over the course of a two-year mission, performing detailed visual inspections.

But Otter 24C never got the chance to perform any of these orbital rendezvous.

"While working through commissioning steps, Starfish eventually stopped receiving data from Otter 24C," the company said in a Nov. 3 X post.

"An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by [California company] Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications," Starfish added. "Starfish, NASA, and Astro Digital have concluded that Otter 24C is not recoverable."

The company further said that it's implementing fixes to reduce the chances that the problem will crop up in the future. And it stressed that Otter 24C's death will not be in vain.

"The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions, as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit," Starfish said.

Otter Pup 2 is now operating as close as 25 meters away from @GilmourSpace's ElaraSat, fully autonomously. This vid contains imagery captured when we were separated by just 33.6 meters. We’ve demonstrated our ability to safely and precisely operate at very close range, executing intricate maneuvers, gathering detailed imagery, and testing the capabilities we’ll need for docking. With this progress, Otter Pup 2 has officially completed Characterize, the penultimate phase of its mission. That leaves just one phase left: attempting docking, and a chance to make history.October 27, 2026

The Seattle company has other work to do in LEO at the moment as well: Its Otter Pup 2 prototype craft is currently gearing up to conduct a historic docking of its own in LEO.

Otter Pup 2, which launched in June 2025, has been getting closer and closer to another private spacecraft, Gilmour Space's ElaraSat. Last week, the company announced that Otter Pup 2 got within a mere 82 feet (25 meters) of its target.

"With this progress, Otter Pup 2 has officially completed Characterize, the penultimate phase of its mission. That leaves just one phase left: attempting docking, and a chance to make history," Starfish Space said in an Oct. 27 X post.

Two private satellites have docked before, but only much higher above Earth, in geostationary orbit. Such a meetup has not yet happened in LEO.

#784. Scientists solve 30-year-old mystery and discover a hidden defense against inflammation

Scientists have solved a biological mystery that remained unanswered for more than three decades, uncovering an unexpected way the immune system protects the body from its own inflammatory response. The breakthrough reveals that a chemical signal responsible for attracting immune cells to fight infections also helps prevent those same defenses from damaging healthy tissue.

The discovery came from researchers at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK), who took an unusual approach to studying inflammation. Rather than relying on mice, a standard choice for biomedical research, they turned to zebrafish. That decision helped them identify a long-mysterious enzyme and uncover a protective mechanism that had previously escaped scientists.

The findings, published October 7 in Nature, could advance research into cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and asthma. They also raise the possibility of developing treatments that strengthen the body's natural defenses against inflammatory damage.

The mystery began in 1992, when researchers at McGill University investigated a molecule that helps direct immune cells toward sites of infection. Known as 5-oxoETE, or 5-oxo-6,8,11,14-eicosatetraenoic acid, this fatty signaling molecule acts as a chemical alert when the body needs to respond to a threat.

At the time, scientists observed an enzyme that could both produce and break down 5-oxoETE. Enzymes are proteins that help chemical reactions take place, but in this case, researchers could not identify the human gene responsible for making the enzyme.

That missing genetic information created a major obstacle. Without knowing which gene produced the enzyme, scientists could not easily manipulate it in experiments or determine how problems with its activity might contribute to disease. Researchers assigned the enzyme a descriptive name based on its chemical function, but its genetic identity remained unknown for more than 30 years.

The breakthrough finally came through the work of Yanan Ma, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher at MSK's Sloan Kettering Institute. Building on earlier investigations by former lab colleague King Lam Hui, PhD, Ma identified the human gene that produces the enzyme, giving researchers a way to examine its function much more closely.

How the Immune System Can Damage Healthy Cells

Ma works in the laboratory of cell biologist Philipp Niethammer, PhD, whose research examines how cells respond to injuries, infections, and other forms of stress. His team focuses on inflammation, tissue repair, and regeneration, biological processes that also play important roles in cancer and numerous other diseases.

When harmful bacteria enter the body, chemical signals help recruit specialized white blood cells to the affected area. One of those signals is 5-oxoETE, which attracts immune cells equipped to attack invading microorganisms.

Although this response is essential for fighting infections, it carries risks. The substances immune cells release to destroy pathogens can also injure surrounding healthy tissue.

"They flood the site with toxic substances to kill the bacteria," Dr. Niethammer says. "But this can cause damage to healthy cells if it gets out of control."

Niethammer's laboratory had already spent years investigating the molecular reactions involved in 5-oxoETE signaling. Researchers were gradually identifying how the different components of the system worked together, but the unknown enzyme remained a major missing piece.

Why Zebrafish Succeeded Where Mice Could Not

Most biomedical experiments involving animals use mice or rats because their biological systems share many similarities with humans. However, these familiar laboratory animals had a significant limitation for the question Ma and her colleagues wanted to answer.

"Mice and rats are the primary model used in biomedical research," says Dr. Ma, who received a prestigious Marie-Josée Kravis WISE Fellowship in 2023 for her work on the pathway. "It makes sense -- they're mammals, and there's about an 80% overlap between their genes and ours."

Despite those similarities, mice lack a known immune cell receptor capable of recognizing 5-oxoETE. Without that receptor, researchers cannot investigate the complete signaling process in mice.

Zebrafish, however, have retained the necessary biological machinery.

"This means that you can't study the pathway in mice," Dr. Ma says. "But the pathway is intact in fish. So picking the right alternative model was critical to advancing our understanding of how the human body responds."

Using zebrafish allowed the scientists to explore how the signal operates in a living organism and eventually helped reveal a function that had gone unnoticed for decades.

Scientists Finally Identify the Missing Enzyme

Before investigating the process in zebrafish, Ma and Hui began searching for the enzyme's genetic origins using cultured human cells.

They selected several genes that might be responsible and systematically switched them off, looking for changes in the enzyme's activity. One candidate produced a decisive result.

When Ma disabled a gene called DHRS7, the enzyme stopped functioning. The experiment established that DHRS7 was the gene researchers had been searching for since the early 1990s.

Additional tests involving the rodent version of the gene showed almost no enzyme activity. That result was consistent with the absence of the 5-oxoETE receptor in mice, suggesting that rodents had lost key functions associated with this signaling system.

Identifying DHRS7 resolved the long-standing mystery. It also connected Ma's research with a separate investigation underway in the same laboratory, led by postdoctoral researcher Miklos Lengyel, MD, PhD.

"Typically, when you have a paper with two first authors like Yanan and Miklos, there is just one story that two people contributed to equally," Dr. Niethammer says. "But this paper is not like that. In this paper, there are two separate projects led by two different authors that came together as one larger discovery. And I think that's extremely important to note."

A Surprising Result Turns Expectations Upside Down

While Ma investigated the mysterious enzyme, Lengyel was using zebrafish to study colitis, an inflammatory condition affecting the colon. His experiments involved disabling selected genes to understand how they influenced intestinal inflammation.

One experiment produced an especially puzzling outcome.

Lengyel removed a gene called hcar1-4 (the zebrafish version of the human gene OXER1). This gene produces the receptor that recognizes 5-oxoETE and allows cells to respond to its signal.

Because 5-oxoETE helps attract immune cells and initiate inflammation, removing its receptor should theoretically weaken that response.

"So if you remove the receptor that detects the signal, you'd expect less inflammation, not more," Dr. Lengyel says.

Instead, the zebrafish developed intestinal inflammation on their own, even though no infection was present.

The researchers initially considered whether neutrophils, the white blood cells normally recruited by the signal, might be responsible. However, removing those immune cells did not eliminate the inflammation.

This unexpected behavior suggested that the 5-oxoETE pathway was doing something much more complicated than simply activating the immune system.

Disabling an Inflammatory Signal Makes Inflammation Worse

The connection between the two research projects became clear after Ma identified DHRS7 as the gene responsible for producing the enzyme involved in 5-oxoETE signaling.

Lengyel then disabled DHRS7 in zebrafish, preventing the production of the enzyme and disrupting the signaling process.

Based on the molecule's established role in attracting immune cells, the researchers expected inflammation to decrease. Instead, they observed the same surprising pattern seen when the receptor was removed: inflammation increased.

"It made absolutely no sense," Dr. Lengyel says. "I had to prove using several different methods before the rest of the lab was convinced."

The findings pointed to a previously unrecognized function. The signaling pathway did not simply help initiate the immune response. It also appeared to prevent unnecessary damage to healthy cells.

That dual responsibility explained why eliminating the pathway had such an unexpected effect. By disabling the system, scientists had removed not only an inflammatory signal but also an important source of cellular protection.

The Immune System's Hidden Protective Shield

Further experiments revealed how this protection works.

When immune cells attack dangerous microorganisms, they release highly reactive substances that can harm nearby healthy cells. The 5-oxoETE pathway helps tissues withstand this chemical stress, reducing the risk that the body's own defenses will cause unnecessary injury.

"This makes sense when you think about it," Dr. Niethammer says. "These immune cells unleash chemical warfare against a pathogen, and organisms have evolved an elegant way of protecting healthy cells at the same time."

The researchers found that zebrafish intestinal cells became particularly vulnerable when either 5-oxoETE or its Hcar1-4 receptor was missing. Even the normal bacteria living in the intestine produced enough low-level chemical stress to cause problems when this protective system was disabled.

The team traced the cellular protection to a group of enzymes known as NUDIX hydrolases. These enzymes help maintain cellular health by removing damaged DNA building blocks before they can interfere with normal biological processes.

Without the protective signaling pathway, intestinal cells could no longer withstand the chemical stress associated with ordinary gut bacteria. Some cells died, setting off an inflammatory response despite the absence of an invading pathogen.

The results revealed that the body uses the same molecular system both to call immune cells into action and to protect healthy tissue from the consequences.

"As it turns out, this signal isn't just an alarm, it's also a shield," Dr. Niethammer says.

Potential Implications for Cancer and Inflammatory Diseases

Understanding this protective mechanism could have important implications for diseases involving excessive or poorly controlled inflammation.

The 5-oxoETE signaling pathway is known to be disrupted in conditions such as cancer, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and asthma. By identifying its previously unknown protective role, researchers have gained a new perspective on how those disruptions might contribute to tissue damage.

In human cancers, mutations affecting DHRS7 and OXER1 (the human version of hcar1-4) have been identified in tumors of the gastrointestinal tract and uterus.

Research has also linked mutations that prevent OXER1 from functioning properly with poorer outcomes in patients with colorectal, pancreatic, and kidney cancers.

The findings suggest that strengthening the pathway might eventually help healthy tissues tolerate damaging conditions more effectively. One possible application involves protecting the intestine from oxidative stress associated with cancer treatment.

"More research is needed, but there's a possibility that activating the pathway could increase the resilience of the gut to oxidative stress -- which might help counteract damage caused by radiation therapy or chemotherapy," Dr. Lengyel says.

The discovery also has implications for diseases affecting mucosal tissues, the protective linings found in areas such as the intestines and respiratory tract.

In people with IBD, researchers have previously associated lower concentrations of 5-oxoETE in intestinal tissue with worse disease outcomes.

Evidence from asthma research points to another possible protective function. An independent study involving primates found that blocking OXER1 weakened the immune cell response but also caused protective mucus-producing cells in the airways to disappear.

Together, these observations suggest that attempts to suppress inflammation must account for the protective roles certain inflammatory signals perform. However, further research will be necessary to determine whether targeting this pathway can produce safe and effective treatments in humans.

How Physical Injury Activates the Same Defense System

The researchers are also investigating how this signaling pathway responds to physical damage, not just infection or chemical stress.

That aspect of the work is being explored by doctoral student Zaza Gelashvili, MS, who studies how cells detect mechanical forces associated with tissue injury.

When cells experience physical stress, changes to their membranes can initiate the same chain of molecular reactions involved in inflammation.

One early step occurs when stressed cell membranes release arachidonic acid, a fatty molecule that serves as the starting material for producing 5-oxoETE.

Gelashvili, a co-author of the Nature study, led a separate investigation into the molecular signals associated with physical wounds. That research was published in Nature Communications earlier in 2026. His contributions were also recognized with the 2026 Chairman's Prize from the Gerstner Sloan Kettering Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

"There's a mechanical component to the pathway that's upstream of what Yanan and Miklos have been studying," explains Gelashvili, a co-author on the study who led a separate study on physical wound signals that was published in Nature Communications earlier this year; his work was also recognized with the 2026 Chairman's Prize from the Gerstner Sloan Kettering Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences. "You can think of it as the first step in a chain reaction: Physical stress unlocks the raw material, oxidative stress drives the conversion, and DHRS7 amplifies the signal."

The research suggests that the body combines information about different forms of cellular stress to coordinate its response. Physical damage can initiate the process, chemical stress can influence the conversion of signaling molecules, and DHRS7 helps strengthen the resulting signal.

Rather than operating as separate responses, these processes appear to work together to help the body recognize danger while limiting unnecessary harm to healthy cells.

"What we are really studying is a pathway that integrates two completely different kinds of stress -- mechanical and metabolic -- and converts them into a single, coordinated, protective response," Dr. Niethammer says.

Additional researchers contributing to the study were Yohannes Ambaw, Leehyeon Kim, Ritchie Ly, Siyang Peng, Meysoon Quraishi, Tobias Walther, and Robert Farese Jr., all affiliated with MSK.

Financial support came from the National Institutes of Health (R35GM140883); an MSK Basic Research Innovation Award; a Starr Foundation Program for Discovery Science grant; a Tow Foundation fellowship; a Marie-Josée Kravis Women in Science Endeavor (WISE) fellowship; a Crohn's Colitis Foundation Research Fellows Award (1268111); an Experimental Immuno-Oncology Scholars fellowship; and core facility services supported in part by MSK's National Cancer Institute Cancer Center Support grant (P30CA008748).

#783. California votes to give record $8.4 billion to medical research

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Students, researchers and others at the University of California, Los Angeles, have protested over cuts to science funding made by the administration of US President Donald Trump during the past two years.Credit: Robyn Beck/AFP via Getty

Voters in California have approved US$8.4 billion in funding for immunology research — the largest ever infusion of cash for science authorized by a public vote in US history.

The funding proposal, known as Proposition 38, appeared on the ballot for voters in California in last week’s US mid-term elections, but it has taken nearly a week for officials to count enough ballots to declare its success. The state government will pay for the research — which aims to find treatments that harness or re-engineer the body’s immune system to fight illnesses such as cancer and Alzheimer’s disease — by selling state government bonds. (This is unusual for science funding. Bonds are typically reserved to pay for infrastructure projects such as road construction and require the state to pay back its debt with interest.)

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

Supporters of the proposal say that the funding will provide stability for researchers in California, who have been affected by political turmoil. The administration of US President Donald Trump has pushed for massive cuts to science funding; put political appointees in charge of grant decisions at federal science agencies, such as the US National Institutes of Health; and forced policy change at US universities that receive federal funding, including those in California.

The $8.4 billion “is an advantage to California that is unprecedented”, says Antoni Ribas, a cancer researcher and physician at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), who supported Proposition 38. It will make the state “even more of a global hub for immunology research”.

But the proposal has sparked debate. That’s because it calls for giving about half of the funding directly to research institutes — and the only institute that matches the criteria called for in the proposal is one co-founded by Gary Michelson, a billionaire medical-device inventor. He wrote the proposition and donated about $45 million of his own funds to get it placed on the ballot and to campaign for its passage.

“I feel like the voters have been taken advantage of,” says Sarah Hill, a political scientist at California State University, Fullerton, who tracks the state’s ballot measures. Michelson did not respond to Nature’s request for comment before this story was published, but has said elsewhere that he will not personally profit from the bond revenue.

In California, citizens can place proposed laws directly on the election ballot by collecting hundreds of thousands of voter signatures.

The state has funded scientific research through this process before. In 2004, after then-president George W. Bush restricted federal funding for human embryonic stem-cell research, voters in California approved a $3-billion bond to establish the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, which they then voted to replenish with another $5.5 billion in 2020.

A campaign mailer encouraging California voters to support Proposition 38.Credit: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty

“The model works,” Ribas says. Immunologists have been making great strides with medicines, such as personalized treatments called CAR-T therapies, that are revolutionizing care, he says. There has also been a flurry of research into developing vaccines, such as the mRNA shots that have been the target of funding cuts by the Trump administration. Proposition 38 will ensure such research can continue regardless of the political headwinds, Ribas adds.

Around $4 billion from Proposition 38 will fund grants for researchers at select public universities and non-profit institutes in California through a competitive review process. According to the proposal, any commercialized therapies developed through funded research must be sold at a 20% discount to people in California, with 10% of drug royalties returning to the state’s general fund.

#782. Jill Scott & Kehlani Face Off In Crowded R&B Album Category at 2027 Grammys: Our Predictions

At the 2026 Grammys, Leon Thomas emerged victorious in the best R&B album category, fending off fellow nominees GIVĒON (Beloved), Ledisi (The Crown), Teyana Taylor (Escape Room) and Coco Jones (Why Not More?). With a Billboard Hot 100 top 10 hit (“Mutt”) and a near-perfect campaign under his belt, the award was practically Thomas’ to lose. But this year’s field is a lot more competitive.

Three-time Grammy-winning R&B icon Jill Scott is the frontrunner for best R&B album at the 2027 Grammys. To Whom This May Concern, her first full-length offering in 11 years, debuted in the top 10 of seven different Billboard charts, spawned her first Adult R&B Airplay chart-topper in over a decade (“Pressha”) and gave way to an acclaimed headlining tour.

Scott, who was inducted into Billboard’s R&B Hall of Fame earlier this year, will likely be nominated across the R&B field, with select album tracks having non-zero chances of showing up in the rap and American roots categories. She’s been incredibly visible this year — even reprising her iconic role of Sheila Jackson in Why Did I Get Married Again? — but, more importantly, Concern is one of the year’s best albums. In fact, Scott may well break into the general field with an album of the year nomination: At least one R&B album has made the lineup every year this decade except for 2025, and Scott fits the bill of a respected OG who delivered a project that met the moment with a career-redefining album.

Kehlani, who won best R&B song and performance last year for her Hot 100 top 10 hit “Folded” (No. 6), is neck-and-neck with Scott for a nomination here. Her self-titled set reached No. 4 on the Billboard 200 and No. 1 on Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums. Featuring icons like Brandy and Missy Elliott, the set also spawned the Usher-assisted hit “Shoulda Never,” which reached No. 10 on Mainstream R&B/Hip-Hop Airplay. The Oakland singer has re-established herself as a Grammy darling in recent years (she picked up three nods at the 2025 ceremony after a seven-year absence), and she’s also a frontrunner to win best melodic rap performance this year alongside Cardi B for “Safe.”

PJ Morton is currently the male soloist with the most nominations in this category (four), and he’s poised to extend that lead with Saturday Night, the R&B side of his Juneteenth-released double album. Chris Brown could potentially become the male soloist with the second-most nods in this category if he makes the final lineup with Brown (The Chocolate Edition). He won here just two years ago for 11:11 (Deluxe), but that album had the hits, acclaim and passion that Brown — which Pitchfork infamously scored a 1.3 out of 10 — lacks. Working in Brown’s favor is his stadium-conquering joint R&B Tour with Usher, which has reinforced his status as one of the most lucrative touring acts in Black music history. Nonetheless, the rumored, concert-delaying tension between the two stars, coupled with Brown’s recent multimillion-dollar legal battle with his former housekeeper, could turn off voters.

Enter a trio of acts that could become first-time nominees in this category: Masego, The Womack Sisters and Kenyon Dixon. Masego made a grand return with Fix Your Face, his first album in three years, which had minimal chart impact but won lots of love in R&B circles thanks to his headlining tour, his Herbie Hancock-honoring “Recommend” music video and standout cuts like “Breathe,” “Heaven” and “Hello” (with Buju Banton). The Womack Sisters, a girl group consisting of siblings who are the nieces of Bobby Womack and granddaughters of Sam Cooke, could earn a nod here for their self-titled debut studio album. The focus single “If I Let You” has reached No. 11 on Adult Alternative Airplay, and the trio is set to open for select dates on Harry Styles’ stadium-headlining Together, Together tour next spring. Finally, Kenyon Dixon, a five-time Grammy nominee, is seeking his first nod in this category for Ego Ruins Everything. He’s garnered tons of love from more traditional R&B fans (his first three career Grammy nods were all for best traditional R&B performance), and Ego elegantly blends more contemporary flourishes into his soulful sound.

Three ladies who helped define late-2010s and early-2020s R&B also have albums in contention: Ella Mai has only scored one nod in this category, but she could return with Do You Still Love Me?, which spawned the Hot 100 hit “Little Things” (No. 81) and anchored her headlining tour. Similarly, Summer Walker boasts one previous nomination in this category, but it was for her Clear 2: Soft Life EP, which offered a far more stripped-down sound than the radio-ready Finally Over It. Nonetheless, the conclusion to the Atlanta singer’s Over It trilogy posted the biggest Billboard 200 debut by a female R&B artist in 2025, dominated the set list of its accompanying arena-headlining tour and spawned several Hot 100 hits, including “Go Girl” (No. 60), “Robbed You” (No. 58) and “No” (No. 69). Then again, her campaign could be stunted by her ongoing legal dispute with Interscope. Finally, Ari Lennox has inexplicably never earned a Grammy nomination for her own work (her sole nod came from Dreamville’s 2020 best rap album bid for Revenge of the Dreamers III), but she could finally make it happen with Vacancy. The record reached No. 25 on Top R&B Albums and earned considerable acclaim in R&B circles.

Mariah Carey is one legend to look out for. She’s in contention with Here for It All, an album that reached the Billboard 200 top 10 (No. 7), spawned two Adult R&B Airplay chart-toppers in “In Your Feelings” and “Type Dangerous,” and housed “Nothing Is Impossible,” which she performed at the 2026 Milan Cortina Winter Olympics Opening Ceremony. With just five wins across her decade-spanning career, Carey is far from a Grammy darling; she hasn’t been recognized by the Recording Academy since 2009, and R&B voters haven’t awarded her since 2006, when she took home best contemporary R&B album for The Emancipation of Mimi and best female R&B vocal performance for “We Belong Together.”

Other titles to look out for include: Heat the Streets (Elmiene), Love Me for Me (October London), God Must Really Love Me (Tori Kelly), Juniper (Joy Crookes), Eric Bellinger (Eric Bellinger) and Ghosted (Saint Harison)

We’re predicting: To Whom This May Concern (Jill Scott); Kehlani (Kehlani); Fix Your Face (Masego); Saturday Night (PJ Morton); The Womack Sisters (The Womack Sisters)

Kendall Jenner and Jacob Elordi are keeping it cozy.

Meanwhile, Elordi looked equally toasty in a white hoodie, matching sneakers and dark blue jeans. The 29-year-old tucked his newly dyed blonde hair beneath a black beanie, which he covered with the hood of his sweater.

The couple, who first sparked dating rumors in April, matched in sunglasses as they sat on a stoop waiting for their drinks.

At one point during their low-key date, Elordi rested his hand on the supermodel's knee, prompting her to wrap her arms around him and rest her chin on his shoulder. As Jenner, 31, took a phone call, she learned in and gave the Frankenstein actor a quick kiss.

But while the two have slowly but surely been more open to PDA in recent months, with Elordi cheering Jenner on at Paris Fashion Week and before attending the Academy Museum Gala as a couple, they're still very much dedicated to keeping details about their relationship private.

After all, Elordi—who previously dated Joey King, Kaia Gerber and Olivia Jade—doesn't believe in letting a romance play out in public.

“You want it to be genuine and real and have all the feelings of what you read in 1920s literature,” he told Vanity Fair in 2020. “But when people are watching and talking about it, it makes it a little bit difficult.”

They say all good things come to those who wait… and WAIT. Well, the wait for "Robopocalypse" fans might finally be over, as Oscar winners Ron Howard and Akiva Goldsman have announced they're working on a TV adaptation.

It does seem like an eternity since news first broke that Portland-based New York Times bestselling author Daniel H. Wilson’s "Robopocalypse" (Doubleday, 2011) was bought by Steven Spielberg’s DreamWorks SKG for a sci-fi spectacle, with Drew Goddard ("The Martian") brought in to pen the screenplay.

That was back in 2009, and since then the story of a rogue AI named Archos and a hearty band of indigenous people in America’s heartland battling to save humanity from extinction has been placed on Hollywood’s back burner. After numerous stalled starts and director Michael Bay getting involved in 2018, "Robopocalypse" was quietly powered down due to script issues, filmmaker scheduling conflicts, and the enormous budget required.

But now we have been blessed with the news, first broken by The Hollywood Reporter, that Ron Howard ("Apollo 13," "The Da Vinci Code") and Akiva Goldsman ("A Beautiful Mind," "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds") have taken up the mantle of this chilling sci-fi project to develop as a new TV series. And what timing, just as AI fever has gripped the planet with paranoia centered around our eventual robot overlords.

"'Robopocalypse' has all the scale and suspense of a major action story, but what drew me to it are the thought-provoking themes and humanity at its center," Ron Howard shared in a statement.

The cover of 2011's smash sci-fi hit Robopocalypse by Daniel H. Wilson

The cover of the 2014 sequel Robogenesis by Daniel H. Wilson

"Daniel created a future that feels both startling and increasingly plausible, with characters who must figure out what connects us when the technology we rely on turns against us. I am also thrilled to work with Akiva again. We have shared some incredibly meaningful creative experiences, and this feels like the right story to bring us back together."

As a PhD graduate of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute and a future king of the techno-thriller, Wilson was the ideal writer to bring this frightening story to life, and a 2014 sequel titled "Robogenesis" was equally gripping.

The prolific, award-winning writer has since set up a multitude of other Hollywood projects spawned from his catalog of works, including "Amped," "The Clockwork Dynasty," the authorized sequel to Michael Crichton's "The Andromeda Strain," "The Andromeda Evolution," and his 2025 alien invasion novel "Hole in the Sky," still alive at Netflix.

Howard's Imagine Entertainment will partner with Akiva Goldsman's Weed Road Pictures on this episodic adaptation, with Howard attached to direct the pilot episode and Goldsman serving as series showrunner.

"Robopocalypse" marks a creative reunion for the distinguished creators, following their collaborations on "A Beautiful Mind," "Cinderella Man," "The Da Vinci Code," and "Angels & Demons." Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment is slated to executive produce the ambitious show alongside Imagine's Brian Grazer and Jeb Brody and Weed's Rachel Wizenberg and Greg Lessans.

It's too early to tell which streaming service the "Robopocalypse" TV show will be attached to yet. Hopefully the pilot episode wows one of the big names, and we can finally see the "Robopocalypse" adaptation of our dreams.

In the meantime, we'd recommend checking out the original book by Daniel H. Wilson.

Not far into our future, the dazzling technology that runs our world turns against us. Controlled by a childlike—yet massively powerful—artificial intelligence known as Archos, the global network of machines on which our world has grown dependent suddenly becomes an implacable, deadly foe.

#779. Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss

You walk out of the grocery store, ready to head home and make dinner. But as you scan the crowded parking lot, a frustrating question comes to mind. Where did you leave your car? You try to picture the spot, but the memory refuses to surface.

Remembering personal experiences like these depends on episodic memory, which allows us to recall events from our lives. These memories help form the foundation of long-term memory, whether they involve a childhood milestone, such as the first day of elementary school, or something that happened just minutes earlier, like parking your car.

This ability tends to weaken as we grow older. The sights, sounds, and other details associated with past experiences can become increasingly difficult to retrieve. Scientists still do not fully understand why this happens. Although some memory decline is a common part of aging, the changes can become far more severe in people developing Alzheimer's disease.

A new study from researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, offers important clues about what may be happening inside the aging brain. Neuroscientist Omer Sharon and his colleagues, working under the direction of former Berkeley sleep researcher Matthew Walker, discovered a connection between disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, declining memory performance, and the accumulation of tau, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The findings suggest that tau buildup in the brain's frontal cortex is linked to changes in the coordinated electrical activity that helps preserve memories overnight.

"This is the first time we've shown this relationship between tau and how it messes with memory consolidation by attenuating traveling slow waves that originate in the frontal cortex," said Sharon, a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley's Center for Human Sleep Science.

The research was published in Nature Neuroscience.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Store Memories

Sleep involves several distinct stages, each associated with different patterns of brain activity. Rapid eye movement sleep is particularly recognizable because the eyes move beneath closed eyelids and most dreaming takes place during this stage. However, another stage, known as non-REM sleep, is especially important for maintaining healthy brain function.

During this deeper stage of sleep, when dreaming is limited or absent, large groups of neurons briefly become inactive and then active again in a coordinated sequence. These synchronized changes produce slow electrical waves that spread across the brain, typically beginning in the frontal cortex.

"Each slow wave reflects an enormous population of neurons switching off and back on together," Sharon said. "Our study shows that for memory, it's critical that these events cascade in sequence across large parts of the brain. This coordinated shutdown has been observed only during deep sleep, and may be one reason why we sleep."

The researchers found that this carefully organized activity becomes less coordinated as tau accumulates in the aging brain. Instead of traveling together across broad regions, the waves become more scattered and cover shorter distances. These changes are associated with weaker memory consolidation, declining cognitive abilities, and Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Protein Linked to Disrupted Brain Waves

To investigate the relationship, the scientists monitored sleeping brain activity using electroencephalograms (EEGs). They compared cognitively healthy young adults in their early 20s with older participants ranging from their mid-60s to mid-70s.

The differences were striking. In younger participants, groups of slow waves moved together across distances roughly equivalent to the width of a hand on the scalp. Among older adults, the waves typically traveled less far and appeared more independently, rather than moving in coordinated groups.

The team also examined whether these changes were associated with tau accumulation. Working with Dr. William Jagust, a UC Berkeley professor emeritus of public health and neuroscience, the researchers used positron emission tomography (PET) scans to examine the brains of older participants. This imaging technique uses radioactive tracers introduced into the bloodstream to reveal biological activity and the distribution of specific substances.

The scans showed that greater tau buildup in the frontal cortex was associated with a breakdown in the longer traveling waves normally seen during deep sleep.

Importantly, these changes were present in people who had not developed Alzheimer's disease.

"These people did not have Alzheimer's," Sharon said. "They had tau in their brains, but with subclinical impacts. Their memory decline was within the normal range for their age."

Sharon explained that early Alzheimer's related changes can vary considerably in severity. The amount of tau present in the brain is associated with cognitive performance, even when a person's memory abilities remain within the expected range for their age.

Mysterious "Lonely Waves" Linked to Memory Loss

The researchers wanted to determine whether the altered sleep patterns were associated with actual differences in how well people remembered information.

To test this, participants learned pairs of associated words in the evening. The following day, they were asked to recall what they had learned, allowing the scientists to evaluate how effectively the memories had been retained overnight.

Participants whose slow brain waves traveled shorter distances and appeared more isolated generally remembered fewer word associations. The researchers called these disconnected patterns "lonely waves."

The team also tracked a subset of participants over several years to see how their brains changed with time. Among those whose frontal cortex tau levels increased, the slow waves became less coordinated, and their ability to retain newly learned information overnight declined.

These observations provide evidence of a relationship between tau accumulation, changes in deep sleep brain activity, and worsening episodic memory. However, they do not establish that tau buildup directly causes memory loss or that disrupted waves are the mechanism responsible.

Additional Tests Strengthen the Connection

Because PET scans are costly and require specialized facilities, the scientists sought another way to investigate the relationship between Alzheimer's related proteins and sleep activity.

They collaborated with neurologist Yo-El Ju at Washington University in St. Louis to analyze spinal fluid from a separate group of older adults. The goal was to determine whether measurements of Alzheimer's associated proteins would reveal patterns similar to those seen with brain imaging.

Unlike PET scans, the spinal fluid measurements could not identify tau accumulation specifically within the frontal cortex. Nevertheless, the results pointed in the same direction.

People whose sleeping brains produced more isolated slow waves had higher ratios of tau to amyloid, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease, in their spinal fluid.

The consistency between these independent groups and testing methods strengthened the researchers' confidence in the findings.

"It's collected in a totally different place and in a different cohort, so I think that adds to the strength of the evidence," Sharon said.

Together, the sleep recordings, brain scans, spinal fluid analyses, and memory assessments suggest that tau accumulation is associated with a particular disruption of brain activity during deep sleep.

"This longitudinal correlation suggests that Alzheimer's disease pathology is associated with a disruption of this main sleep feature," Sharon said.

What Deep Sleep Reveals About the Aging Brain

Although memory often declines with age, the new research indicates that the process may involve more than simply growing older. Changes associated with Alzheimer's disease, particularly tau accumulation in regions responsible for generating widespread slow waves, may help explain why some people experience greater difficulty retaining memories.

"It's not just about age," Sharon said. "It's how much pathology you have in frontal areas where global waves originate."

Sleep quality also appears to be part of the picture. Although it can be difficult to define or measure precisely, the organization and movement of slow brain waves may provide important indicators of how effectively the brain performs its nighttime memory functions.

The findings raise the possibility that changes in deep sleep activity could eventually help researchers better understand or identify early memory problems. They also point toward potential targets for future treatments aimed at protecting memory as people age.

For now, however, a central question remains unanswered. Scientists still need to determine whether accumulating tau contributes to the breakdown of synchronized sleep waves, whether changes in those waves influence tau accumulation, or whether the relationship involves additional processes.

"We can see tau and lonely waves rising together over time," Sharon said. "What we cannot yet say is which leads -- and that question will shape how we design interventions."

The study's additional co-authors include Xi Chen, James Westphal, Chelsea Brown, and Vyoma D. Shah of UC Berkeley, along with Jason Dude of Washington University in St. Louis.

Funding came from grants awarded by the National Institute on Aging at the National Institutes of Health. Sharon also received support through a Glenn Foundation for Medical Research Postdoctoral Fellowship and a Weill Neurohub Fellowship.

#778. Nicko McBrain on Iron Maiden Missing Its Rock Hall Induction: ‘I’m Sure We’ll Say Thank You In Another Way’

The drummer, who recently retired from the road, is releasing his memoir, Hello Boys and Girls!, ahead of the ceremony.

In his new memoir, Nicko McBrain joyfully cracks open the tight, closed world that is Iron Maiden. And while there’s plenty of metal in its 344 pages, don’t expect to find much in the way of mayhem in Hello Boys and Girls! (HarperCollins), publishing just in front of the band’s induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame on Saturday (Nov. 14). Explore Iron Maiden See latest videos, charts and news

“I intentionally steered away from the debauchery; there’s a fair share in there, but I wanted it to be more classy, this story,” the London-born drummer — who joined Maiden during 1982 and retired from touring with the band in December 2024 — tells Billboard via Zoom from his home in Boca Raton, Fla. “We were very young, very proud, very crazy. There were a lot of drugs. The sex, we had our fair share – yeah, we did — but I didn’t want the book to reflect that. I wanted it to be more passionate, more reflective of the story rather than going into the gutter…’cause we weren’t in it for the sex and drugs and the money. That was never the drive and the passion behind Iron Maiden, and it’s the same today.” Related Bella Kay Teases New Music In Billboard 'Up & Coming' Podcast Series Premiere: 'It's Kinda Giving Deluxe' It's Looking Like Oasis Will Skip Their Own Rock Hall of Fame Induction: 'It's Too Far To Be Going For the Night' Brothers Osborne, Luke Bryan, Vince Gill, Halestorm & More Added As 2026 CMA Awards Performers

McBrain adds, “You have to bear in mind that (now) everybody is married and has their own families and children who, goodness gracious, are all grown up. So I steered clear, intentionally, of most of the stories that involved the debauchery.” He adds with a laugh that “there are certain stories to be told. Maybe that’ll be another book!”

All that said, Hello Boys and Girls! is still an entertaining and engaging rock ‘n’ roll read. Co-written with Benjamin Dirs (Geezer Butler’s Into the Void), it captures McBrain’s jovial and conversational demeanor and outlook, laughing at the world around him — and often at himself. It also illuminates how a youngster blown away by Dave Brubeck Quartet drummer Joe Morello’s “Take Five” solo on the BBC became a career player himself.

That includes several eventful stops before McBain made it into Maiden in 1982 — including sessions for guitarist Gordon Giltrap and membership in Streetwalkers, Pat Travers’ band and the French group Trust, whose frequent food fights, on any occasion and any locale, provide some of the book’s funniest moments.

“I thought the main reason to write this story was because there’s so much that happened prior to Iron Maiden,” he says, “With great bands, players and musicians. So the inspiration was all of the stories prior to Maiden, and then we get to the nitty-gritty stuff. But it isn’t a book just about my lifetime spent in the ranks of Iron Maiden — 42 years, that’s a long time and a blessing as well. But the inspiration was I wanted to write my story about my life, and of course the majority of it is Iron Maiden stories.”

One thing that’s abundantly clear in Hello Boys and Girls! is that, alongside wife Rebecca — whom McBrain calls “my true north star” in the dedication — drums are, in fact, the love of his life.

“Absolutely,” he acknowledges. “I think it was the ferocity, the voracious stamina that (Morello) had when I saw that solo. I was 10 and a half years old. The ‘Take Five’ groove in itself, I’d never heard anything like that, in the odd time. I always thought 1-2-3-4, 2-2-3-4…So hearing a 5/4 drum fill and the music being played, I’m like, ‘What is this?’ Then he went off into the solo, and I’m like, ‘That’s what I want to do, dad! I’m gonna be a drummer!'”

McBrain says the book has been a long time coming. He had a publishing deal more than dozen years ago and was 20 or so chapters in when he “hit a brick wall” — partly due to Maiden commitments — and elected to give his advance payment back. But when he decided to retire after suffering a stroke in 2023, the band’s management revived the idea and helped him move the project forward. Maiden bassist and founder Steve Harris, he says, was also encouraging. “I took away a humbleness while I was writing,” McBrain says. “The whole time I thought, ‘Be humble, mate. Just tell the story.’ I was told off about a couple of things by (manager Rod Smallwood) — ‘Oh, no, you can’t be writing about that’ and I went, ‘Sorry, Rod; this is my story.'”

Hello Boys and Girls! follows Maiden guitarist Adrian Smith’s 2020 Monsters of River and Rock, which dealt as much with his passion for fishing as it did music. As of this interview, McBrain is waiting for Maiden members’ reactions to his book.

“I’m not sure if any of the band has seen it; I think if they have I’ll be getting a bollocking, a phone call: ‘You shouldn’t be saying that!'” he says with another laugh. “I think Steve might have had a little look at it, but I haven’t actually spoken to him about it. When the speaking tour I’m doing  all sold out, he sent me a note: ‘Well done. Congratulations. Knock ’em dead.'”

Nearly two years after his final concert with the group, McBrain — who now plays in a Maiden tribute band called Titanium Tart — says that “I dearly miss the camaraderie of my brothers every day. I don’t miss the travel (but) I miss the fans, the interaction at a live show and the interaction on the days off when Janick (Gers, guitarist) and I would have a wander around the city we were in and get to see the fans and meet them. I miss that. I miss the crew. And I miss the feeling of sitting behind my drum set and playing and driving the band.” But he’s had no second thoughts or regrets about his decision.

“I am grateful and praise God every day for giving me this wonderful life I’ve had,” says McBrain, adding that he’s in good health — “just normal aches and pains of being an old git” — and taking “proactive” care of himself since the stroke. He has not seen Iron Maiden live since he retired, partly in deference to current touring drummer Simon Dawson (from Harris’ other band, British Lion). McBrain says he hopes “to do a couple of songs” on the next Maiden album, though there are no concrete plans yet for a follow-up to 2021’s Senjutsu, which became their highest-charting album on the Billboard 200 upon its release.

“Because of my handicap, it would have to be a song like ‘Stranger in a Strange Land’ or ‘Number of the Beast,'” McBrain says, “Something that’s not got large drum fills and drum motifs in them, ’cause I wouldn’t be able to play them. I went to dinner with Bruce (Dickinson, frontman) last year and I said, ‘Are you gonna do a new record?’ and he looked at me and said, ‘What do you think?’ Knowing Bruce, that’s what he wants. And I did talk to Steve, and it was like, ‘Maybe.’ So at this moment there’s no plans to do a new record, but watch this space, ironmaiden.com. That’s all I can say.”

McBrain says he was willing to represent Maiden at the Rock Hall induction in Los Angeles while the band tours Australia, but his speaking tour in Europe, which kicked off Oct. 26 in Germany, will keep him across the pond through early December. (He’s also added a Dec. 8 appearance at the Barnes & Noble store in Boca Raton, Fla.) He’s nevertheless “personally very honored” by the induction, despite Maiden’s professed ambivalence about the institution.

“It’s taken a long time for the band to be recognized,” McBrain says. “There was a time when I agreed with Bruce and said, ‘This is a load of kerfuffle. We don’t even want to entertain thinking about it.’ That was way back; now we’re moving forward, and there have been changes within the powers that be and I think they’re more listening to what the fans want. Now, I think to have an accolade and be honored like that, it’s great. I would’ve gone in a heartbeat, but I’m on tour and the boys are in Australia. I’m sure we’ll say thank you in another way.”

McBrain’s remaining author appearances include:

Nov. 13 — DR Studio 2, Copenhagen, Denmark

Nov. 15 — Malta Music Festival, St. Julian’s, Malta

Dec. 8 — Barnes & Noble, Boca Raton, Fla.
