Sosa is a star on-and-off the ballroom floor, being regarded as one of the first pros to reintroduce the online audience to DWTS alongside Rylee Arnold. Now, after capping off his third season with movie star Stiles, Sosa has more than an understanding on what it takes to be a pro; he embodies the essence of what it means to be a DWTS professional dancer, possessing the dance skills and social media savviness needed to lead the show.

Below, Sosa exclusively chats with THR after he and Stiles’ season 35 elimination, breaks down how their 10 Things I Hate About You cast reunion came about, how he manages the growing fan criticism about the show, and who he’s rooting for the win the Len Goodman mirrorball trophy.

What have the past few days been like for you post elimination?

It’s very interesting, because I’m a very single girly, so I feel like the only relationships I do defer to are the ones that I’ve maintained throughout the show. The day after [being eliminated] just feels like a breakup. That’s literally the only way to describe it.

I feel very content with my season with Julia. Like, yes, we could have made it farther, but also, we had such strong moments. I’m just gonna miss her. I feel like that first day [after being eliminated,] we got our tattoos, we said our goodbyes. It was a very bittersweet day, but also was a nice day to reflect on the whole season.

Now, after each season, you have this tradition of getting a tattoo. Why is it important for you to continue that tradition?

I feel like it just happened to become a tradition. I feel like with Anna Delvey, I wanted to have fun with the bit, and with Jordan [Chiles], she already has tattoos, so I feel like it was a comment, “OK, let’s get tattoos.” And the same with Julia, but actually Julia wanted to do it because she is a fan of the show and a fan of mine, so I feel like it was part of her dream inspo to be on Dancing With the Stars and get matching tattoos with me. I feel like that’s really cool to even say and do.

I also feel like it’s a great way to find closure within your season, but also have something to remember the season. I’m very passionate about every single season I’ve been on as a pro, so for me, it’s a way to be proud of the work that I did.

You penned such a beautiful tribute in honor of Julia. Can you open up about what was different about this season with Julia?

Julia is a class act. I’ve never met someone with such star power like Julia. She still is a superstar, but at the height of her career, that was a time in Hollywood that wasn’t on social media, so it was very interesting to collaborate with her on so many different things, including social media. It really was so special.

This is your third season on the show, but you have really tapped into the professional part of the word “professional dancer”. What has it been like growing as a pro these past three seasons? It feels like you have a nail on what it means to be a pro dancer in the new era of Dancing With the Stars.

Well, thank you so much. That means a lot. For me, it’s ultimately about catering the best experience for your partner. Throughout every partnership I’ve had, I’ve also adapted and changed because I am a person that’s constantly learning and growing. With every single partner — and I mean every partner I’ve had — I’ve taken little life lessons that have adjusted the way I look at life, the way I look at dance, and I think that’s a beautiful part of being a reoccurring thing on Dancing With the Stars.

I never want to be the same person every single season, so it’s cool to see how I went from unhinged Anna to completely 180 with Julia, giving all this nostalgia in the world. With Julia, she taught me so, so much about, I mean, professionalism is a light way to say it, but she is a true professional.

Can you clarify; were you part-time living in New York and flying back-and-forth for the shows in L.A.?

Yeah, so it depends on the week. Some weeks we had to be in L.A., like the group dance, we obviously wanted to be here. I loved the fact that Julia just wanted to be with her kids and family [in New York]. I feel like that was a really big thing for her to do the show. I feel like she kind of felt bad for me to be flying back and forth, but I told her, “Whatever is going to give you more ease every single day, I will gladly bend my back for you,” because again, it’s all about their experience on the show.

That had to have been a huge part of the season for you guys, going back and forth and having to travel. Why do you think that wasn’t highlighted on the show? Because fans online [somewhat] knew, but it wasn’t really showcased in your story on the show.

(Laughs.) I’m honestly not sure. I don’t really know what production, like what their motives are. But I definitely feel like when it came to those weeks [when we were traveling] for us specifically, Julia and I, it was more important to talk about the intention of the dance or what we wanted to talk about in our package that week. And majority of times, it didn’t really necessarily come to us [talking about] traveling back and forth.

You choreographed two numbers this season that honored these two major movies. What was that experience like choreographing those numbers in honor of these movies?

A moment I’ll never forget is at the end of her dedication performance, just seeing her reunited with the 10 Things I Hate About You cast. I remember sitting there, full body chills, and just thinking to myself, Oh, this is for sure my peak. There’s nothing that can top this. But even for someone like me who was a huge fan of those movies, it was so important to have so much care behind those two pieces. Ultimately, they became some of my favorite routines that I’ll ever have the chance to perform on Dancing With the Stars, and in general. It’s really cool to be a part of something that I think the ballroom will never forget for years to come.

Whose idea was that to do the 10 Things I Hate About You cast reunion? Was it you? Was it Julia? Was production?

It was Julia. Production opened up Dedication Night so the person [being paid tribute in the dance] could have been passed. It was really important to us to do this dedication performance, not just to Heath, but to that time of her life and filming 10 Things I Hate About You, but we had to think of a person that kind of tied it in. And they’re like, “Were there writers?” I’m looking at her, I was like, “Was there someone in the cast?” She goes, “It has to be the whole cast.” And from there, she started working. She started reaching out to everybody, and Joseph Gordon-Levitt said yes. After that, everyone kind of fell into place.

Are you able to share what song you would have performed to for Grammy night?

It was going to be an Adele song. We were very excited about it because she notoriously doesn’t really clear much [of her music for usage], so it was truly an honor for us to get that clearance. The rumba would have been such a beautiful routine, but you know, just wasn’t in the cards for us. And I’m sure everything happens for a reason.

What do you think was your favorite number you and Julia performed?

It’s hard just to pick one, but I think personally, the “Jenny from the Block” routine was such a fun routine, such a great way to get Julia accustomed to the ballroom. But also, like, should there have been jazz in that routine? Absolutely, but [it was fun] just to do something for the millennials. Like, the intention of it wasn’t necessarily for the ballroom, it was like a love letter for all the millennials. That was a really fun idea to come up with. We were originally supposed to do another style that week, and we were gonna reference her movie Save the Last Dance that week.

There’s just so many eyes on DWTS right now, and with that comes a lot of criticisms and conversations about the show. Is there any conversation in particular that has been sparked this season that has particularly stood out to you?

I definitely feel like everyone loves their opinions on Dancing With the Stars, and we, of course, being a public show, wed allow it and we love it, and we love hearing the audiences’ reactions to the show. But there has been a part of the season that kind of felt a little bit heavier, and maybe it’s because the pros are too lethal at their jobs. I feel like the expectation when it comes to delivering these numbers is just extra high, and that pressure was definitely felt this season amongst everyone in the cast.

But in a weird way, when it came to all the outside noise, and this is, I feel like, the silver lining between it all, it brought us closer together behind the scenes. I can confidently say we have not been this close. All the pros have rehearsals at seven in the morning, and you think seven in the morning with your coworkers is your biggest nightmare, but it is genuinely one thing that I look forward to every single week. We all just get to recap our weeks, and there’s no other person that can relate to what we go through than each other.

So I feel like yes, the outside noise has been a little bit louder, and it has their opinions, and yes, those things are very hard for us to deal with because it is a stress that all of us go through on the show. It’s kind of beautiful to see how it genuinely did bring us all together.

How early do you start preparation for tour?

Actually, pretty early. I think we have 10 days off between season [35] ends and the tour [prep] starts. It’s very important to make sure when we go out there on the road, the show is absolutely spectacular. So our rehearsal process is a pretty long process, but I also think it’s long so it’s less harder on our bodies. I’m really excited for tour. It’s gonna be so awesome. All arenas, Madison Square Garden, sold out.

Now that you are eliminated, who are you rooting for to win the mirrorball?

It’s no shade to the male celebrities on the show because they’re absolutely great; I’m a queen, so I’m gonna be supporting my girls. I feel like being in the group dance with Tatyana [Ali], Amber [Glenn] and Maura [Higgins] — and obviously, we felt like this [reaches arm out] with Jenna Dewan, like, You’re with us! You’re with the girlies! — it was nice to see all of them bond together and have shared, similar experiences on the show. After that, I’m like, girl, I’m rooting for you all. I’m rooting for all my girlies, but I still have much love for the male celebrities on the show.

Season 35 of DWTS airs Tuesdays at 8 p.m., simulcasting across ABC and Disney+, and streaming the next day on Hulu. Read all of THR‘s DWTS coverage here.

#750. A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer

For nearly 50 years, scientists have struggled to explain why frogs began disappearing from Brazil's Atlantic Forest, one of the world's richest regions for amphibian diversity. Beginning in the 1970s, researchers documented dramatic population declines, but the cause of these losses remained uncertain.

Now, scientists have uncovered compelling evidence pointing to a deadly fungal disease as the likely explanation. The findings, published in Molecular Ecology, come from researchers at the Center for Conservation Genomics at the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (NZCBI) and Pennsylvania State University (PSU).

The suspected culprit is chytridiomycosis, often called chytrid, a disease caused by the microscopic fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis. Scientists believe the pathogen originated in Asia before spreading around the world during the 1970s and 1980s. However, the fungus was not formally identified and described until 1999, long after devastating amphibian declines had begun.

By then, hundreds of amphibian species worldwide had been driven toward extinction, and some had already disappeared. Because so many populations collapsed before scientists knew the fungus existed, determining whether it was responsible has been particularly difficult.

"After almost 50 years, we still aren't confident what caused many historical amphibian die-offs, making these declines some of the most enduring cold cases in wildlife epidemiology," said Jack Boyette, an NZCBI graduate fellow and doctoral candidate at PSU who led the research.

A 50-Year-Old Mystery in Brazil's Atlantic Forest

One of these longstanding mysteries centers on the Boracéia Biological Station in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, where amphibian populations experienced severe declines between 1979 and 1982.

Some researchers previously suggested that climate change or unusually extreme weather might have triggered the disappearances. The new findings, however, provide evidence that an emerging fungal disease was spreading through the area at precisely the same time.

"While environmental factors could have played a role, our findings most directly implicate the chytrid fungus, revealing that regional invasion of the pathogen coincided with these unexplained amphibian disappearances," Boyette said.

To investigate what happened, the researchers turned to an unexpected source of evidence: frogs preserved in museum collections decades earlier.

The Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History houses specimens collected by William Ronald Heyer, a former curator of amphibians and reptiles. Heyer conducted five collecting expeditions at Boracéia, including two during the 1970s before the major population declines and three during the 1980s after the die-offs had occurred.

These preserved animals offered scientists a rare opportunity to examine the period before and after the mysterious disappearances. By testing specimens collected at different times, researchers could investigate when the pathogen arrived and how rapidly it spread.

The team analyzed samples from more than 370 preserved amphibians representing 17 species, searching for evidence of chytrid infection and tracking how frequently the fungus appeared over time.

Museum Specimens Reveal a Deadly Fungal Outbreak

The results revealed a striking change. None of the specimens collected before 1979 showed evidence of chytrid infection. Among those collected during the 1980s, however, more than half tested positive for the fungus.

This sharp increase suggests that the pathogen arrived and spread through the local amphibian community around the same time that frog populations were collapsing.

But the researchers also uncovered a surprising pattern.

Species that suffered the most severe declines showed no detectable signs of infection in the preserved specimens. Meanwhile, species whose populations remained relatively stable frequently carried the fungus.

At first glance, these findings might seem to contradict the idea that chytrid caused the disappearances. The researchers believe the explanation may lie in differences in how individual species respond to the disease.

Some frogs may have been naturally capable of tolerating the infection, allowing them to survive even when the fungus was present. More vulnerable species, on the other hand, may have died so quickly after becoming infected that few or no infected individuals were ever collected.

"It's important to keep in mind that not all species suffered catastrophic losses at Boracéia," Boyette said. "The species that didn't decline may have naturally tolerated the fungus, allowing them to become infected without suffering mass mortality. By contrast, the species that declined most dramatically may have been so susceptible that infected frogs died before Heyer could collect them."

Together, the results suggest that chytrid spread rapidly among frogs with little previous exposure to the disease, with potentially devastating consequences for species unable to withstand infection.

Decades-Old Collections Help Solve a Wildlife Cold Case

For Michael Campana, a genomicist at NZCBI who contributed to the research, the findings demonstrate the extraordinary scientific value of natural history museums.

Specimens preserved many decades ago can contain biological evidence that researchers at the time had no way of recognizing. Modern testing methods now make it possible to revisit these collections and investigate outbreaks that occurred long before the responsible pathogens were discovered.

"Museum collectors could not have anticipated how important their collections would be to our modern conservation challenges, but without them, we would never be able to detect pathogens that went unnoticed for decades and reconstruct disease outbreaks that would otherwise remain a mystery," Campana said.

Understanding these past outbreaks could also help scientists anticipate future threats.

One growing concern involves another fungal pathogen, B. salamandrivorans, which is threatening salamander populations in Europe and could pose a serious danger to salamanders in North America.

By reconstructing how earlier fungal diseases emerged, spread, and affected different species, researchers hope to improve their ability to recognize and respond to similar threats before they cause widespread damage.

Brazil's Frogs Show Surprising Signs of Recovery

Despite the devastating losses recorded decades ago, the latest findings also offer encouraging evidence of recovery.

Working with researchers from the University of São Paulo, the team made six visits to Boracéia between 2022 and 2024 to investigate the amphibians living there today.

Of the 17 species represented in Heyer's historical museum collection, researchers located 12 during their modern surveys. The remaining five were not found, leaving their current status uncertain and raising concerns that some may have disappeared from the site entirely.

Nevertheless, the surveys indicate that most amphibian species at Boracéia have recovered since the severe declines of the early 1980s.

The fungus has not disappeared. Chytrid infections are still present among local frogs, but the pattern of infection suggests that species once heavily affected by the disease may have developed greater tolerance over successive generations.

That increased tolerance could help explain why many populations have survived and rebounded despite continuing exposure to the pathogen.

The findings highlight an important distinction between infection and mortality. A species can carry a dangerous pathogen without necessarily suffering catastrophic losses, particularly if its members can tolerate the infection.

What the Discovery Means for Future Amphibian Survival

Although the evidence strongly implicates chytrid in the historic declines at Boracéia, the researchers caution that their findings apply to this particular location. The results cannot automatically explain amphibian disappearances elsewhere in the Atlantic Forest.

Still, the study provides a compelling explanation for a longstanding local mystery and demonstrates how scientists can use historical specimens to reconstruct outbreaks that would otherwise remain poorly understood.

Researchers are now examining DNA recovered from museum specimens to identify the genetic mechanisms that influenced how amphibians responded to chytrid infections in the past. These analyses could help reveal why some species were devastated while others survived.

Separate projects are using ancient environmental DNA to help fill gaps in historical specimen records. This approach involves searching for genetic traces left behind by organisms in their surroundings, potentially providing evidence of species and pathogens that were never directly collected.

Together, these efforts could reveal a much clearer history of how chytrid emerged, spread, and affected amphibian biodiversity over the past century.

By uncovering the biological changes that helped some frogs survive and recover, scientists may also gain valuable insights into protecting vulnerable species from future fungal epidemics.

In his World view, Marc Schmitt argues that if universities teach students to argue with artificial-intelligence systems and assess their debating skills, and if developers offer learning modes, then students will use such tools as a sparring partner rather than as an oracle (see Nature 657, 575; 2026). From six minutes of darkness in Egypt or totality over the Australian Outback, here are the pros and cons of the next two total solar eclipses.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For those who want to experience a total solar eclipse, the next two years present the best kind of problem. On Aug. 2, 2027, the so-called "eclipse of the century" will sweep across southern Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, bringing more than six minutes of totality to parts of Egypt. Then, on July 22, 2028, another exceptionally long total solar eclipse will cross Australia, putting the remote Outback and Sydney Harbor in the path of the moon's dark central shadow before it reaches New Zealand's beautiful South Island.

Both eclipses will be spectacular, and both will require careful planning, yet they promise very different experiences. The 2027 event combines over six minutes of totality with some of the very best weather prospects possible, while 2028 offers over five minutes of totality above some of the world's most famous wildernesses and cityscapes.

Eclipse chasing requires careful planning and dedication, but also significant funds. If you can only choose one, which should it be?

On paper, 2027 is difficult to beat. Maximum totality on Aug. 2 will last about 6 minutes, 23 seconds, making it the longest totality on land since 1991 and until 2114. The path of totality will cross southern Spain and Gibraltar before sweeping across Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Sudan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Somalia and the Chagos Islands. About 88.9 million people live in its path, according to Time and Date. It will dominate the news for weeks.

For Europeans, southern Spain is the obvious easy option. Tarifa, at the country's southern tip, will see about 4 minutes, 39 seconds of totality, while the U.K. Overseas Territory of Gibraltar gets about 4 minutes, 25 seconds. Travel farther east and the duration increases, with Sfax in Tunisia getting around 5 minutes, 41 seconds and locations in Egypt experiencing more than six minutes. Weather prospects generally improve, too, as the path crosses the deserts of North Africa.

Egypt is the headline destination. Luxor will see about 6 minutes, 20 seconds of totality near midday, with Karnak Temple, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the world's greatest ancient monuments nearby. The climatic odds are excellent, with clouds extremely rare in early August. That combination of a very long totality, ancient landscapes and a very high probability of a clear sky makes 2027's path of totality highly unusual.

But there are downsides. Temperatures around Luxor can exceed 105°F (41°C) in August, a dust storm is not impossible, and totality occurs shortly after 1 p.m. when the sun (and moon) will be high overhead — making photography very difficult. Demand is already intense, making organized trips expensive. Spain will be considerably easier and probably cheaper for European eclipse chasers, but at the expense of roughly two minutes of totality — and slightly less favorable weather prospects.

If 2027 is about extreme duration, 2028 is about choice. On July 22, 2028, a path of totality will cross the Cocos Islands, Christmas Island, Australia, from northwest to southeast — passing directly over Sydney — before continuing across the Tasman Sea to New Zealand's South Island. That's about 6.3 million people, according to Time and Date. This will be an exclusive eclipse experienced by relatively few people, certainly when compared to the eclipses in 2024, 2026 and 2027.

Maximum totality will last 5 minutes and 10 seconds in the remote Kimberley region of Western Australia. That's more than a minute shorter than 2027, but still exceptionally long by total solar eclipse standards (most last about two minutes). More importantly, the Australian Outback has excellent climatic prospects. Historical cloudiness on July 22 is around 8% at Purnululu (Bungle Bungles) close to the point of greatest eclipse in Western Australia and 19% at Karlu Karlu (Devil's Marbles) in the Northern Territory, making Australia's interior an attractive destination for serious eclipse chasers. Temperatures will be around 86°F (30°C) in July.

Then there's Sydney. Australia's largest city will experience about 3 minutes, 45 seconds of totality, its first total solar eclipse since 1857. Sydney Opera House and Harbor Bridge beneath a totally eclipsed sun could produce some of the decade's defining astronomical images, while millions of people experiencing totality together should create an extraordinary atmosphere. Temperatures will be around 62.6°F (17°C).

A compromise is weather. Historical cloudiness in Sydney is around 43%, which is good odds for most eclipses — and July is known for clear weather. But in 2028, anyone prioritizing their chances of a clear totality will be tempted by a (albeit pricier) trip to the Outback. For Europeans, reaching Australia also comes with considerable cost and time. The huge number of hotels in Sydney could keep accommodation relatively competitive, but the long flight means it makes little sense to travel there for only a few days. For many international eclipse chasers, 2028 will naturally become an expensive one- or two-week trip.

There's another reason to think beyond those few minutes of darkness. With the right planning, an eclipse trip can also become an extraordinary astronomy vacation (tip: come a week before the eclipse for the darkest evening skies). Here, 2028 offers visitors from Europe and North America something very different — the Southern Hemisphere night sky.

July is a superb time to see the bright central regions of the Milky Way from dark locations in Australia. The Southern Cross, or Crux, is one of the southern sky's defining sights, with Alpha and Beta Centauri nearby. Omega Centauri, the largest and brightest globular cluster visible from Earth, is another showpiece, while the Eta Carinae region offers one of the richest sections of the Milky Way for binoculars and small telescopes.

There are other reasons to extend the trip. A partial lunar eclipse occurs on July 6-7, 2028, while the Southern Delta Aquariid meteor shower peaks around July 28 — a week after the eclipse, during a first-quarter moon — and is particularly well seen from the Southern Hemisphere. Add Australia's world-class dark skies, and a trip into the Outback could become as much about stargazing as the eclipse itself.

The 2027 eclipse has fewer night-sky extras. The Delta Aquariid meteor shower peaks a few days before the eclipse — in dark, moonless skies — while Jupiter will dominate the western sky shortly after sunset. However, anyone traveling from the Northern Hemisphere will largely see a familiar celestial hemisphere. Australia offers a genuinely different sky experience.

Perhaps the most useful way to choose between these eclipses is not to compare their durations, but to imagine where you would most like to be when the moon's shadow arrives.

In 2027, the decision largely comes down to how far along the eclipse track you want to travel. Stay in southern Spain for convenience and around four minutes of totality, head into Tunisia for longer totality and excellent weather prospects, or go all-in on Egypt for more than six minutes beneath almost cloudless desert skies — and bragging rights among eclipse chasers. It's an eclipse that can be combined with beaches, Roman ruins, North African cities or the temples and, of course, the tombs of ancient Egypt.

In 2028, the contrast is even greater. Sydney offers a communal total solar eclipse — a busy "we eclipse" — with millions watching daylight disappear above one of the world's great cities. Head thousands of miles away into the Australian interior and the same event becomes a lonely "me eclipse" in the wilderness, with up to five minutes of totality above an immense Outback landscape. Continue to New Zealand, and there's yet another possibility — a shorter totality with the sun much lower in the afternoon sky.

If your priority is purely totality duration, 2027 marginally wins. More than six minutes of totality combined with extraordinarily reliable weather is a rare combination. There's a good reason Aug. 2, 2027 is being marketed as the "eclipse of the century." But if you've always wanted to visit Australia or New Zealand, the 2028 eclipse is an extraordinary excuse to finally go, in addition to experiencing a long totality.

Choose the trip you most want to take, then find the best possible place for you within the path of totality. After all, no total solar eclipse lasts long enough, and most eclipse chasers struggle to recall exactly how long totality lasted. They're just left with the same question as always — when is the next one?

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#747. Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success

For decades, explanations for why some children struggle with reading have often focused on two factors: intelligence and the ability to process visual information. Children who read easily have frequently been assumed to be more intelligent, while those who struggle have sometimes been viewed as less capable. Another common belief is that reading difficulties arise primarily from problems interpreting the words and letters on a page.

However, a major new study challenges these assumptions, suggesting that the abilities most important for reading success may be very different from what many people expect.

Dr. Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor in Texas A&M University's Department of Educational Psychology, led one of the most extensive investigations to date into how cognitive abilities relate to reading performance. The research brought together scientists from the University of Kansas, St. John's University, Montclair State University and Temple University to examine which mental skills best predict reading development and why some children encounter difficulties.

Massive Study Reveals What Really Predicts Reading Success

To investigate these relationships, the researchers combined 50,000 correlations drawn from 137 cognitive and achievement test batteries into a single statistical model. This large-scale approach allowed them to assess the contribution of individual mental abilities to reading performance while also helping clarify why previous studies had sometimes produced conflicting conclusions.

The findings revealed several surprises. Visual processing showed no meaningful relationship with reading ability across the analysis. General intelligence was associated with reading performance, but its influence was considerably smaller than some earlier research had suggested.

Instead, two less frequently discussed abilities emerged as particularly important predictors of reading success: auditory processing and comprehension-knowledge.

"One notable finding was that general intelligence was less dominant than in some earlier meta-analyses," Hajovsky said. "Broad abilities such as comprehension-knowledge and auditory processing played strong, specific roles in reading beyond general intelligence, especially for decoding and comprehension."

Two Overlooked Skills Play a Major Role in Reading

Auditory processing involves recognizing and distinguishing the individual sounds that make up spoken words. For example, a child needs to identify the separate sounds within a word to understand how those sounds correspond to written letters. This skill helps support decoding, the process of working out how written words are pronounced.

Comprehension-knowledge refers to the vocabulary, concepts and background information a child has accumulated through learning and everyday experiences. Having this foundation makes it easier to understand the meaning of words, sentences and longer passages.

Together, these two abilities were more reliable predictors of reading performance than any other skills examined in the study. Other cognitive functions, including memory, reasoning and mental processing speed, also contributed to reading development, although they played more supporting roles.

The results suggest that reading is not simply a reflection of overall intelligence or how effectively a child processes visual information. Instead, it depends on several interconnected abilities, with language-related skills playing especially important roles.

What the Findings Mean for Children Who Struggle to Read

The research could help educators better understand why individual students experience reading difficulties. Rather than treating all reading problems as the same, teachers may be able to identify particular weaknesses and provide instruction that addresses those needs.

For families, the findings also offer an encouraging message. A child who has trouble reading is not necessarily less intelligent or incapable of becoming a strong reader. Difficulties may instead reflect specific abilities that need additional development and support.

"Strengthening foundational skills at home, even the ones that seem simple, can have meaningful effects on more advanced reading abilities," Hajovsky said. "Struggles in reading are not a sign of low ability but often reflect one specific skill that needs strengthening within a larger system that works together."

The findings highlight the value of helping children build essential reading skills through consistent support, both in the classroom and at home.

According to Hajovsky, the most effective approach involves cooperation among schools, parents, and communities. Reading develops through a network of connected skills, and strengthening those foundations one step at a time can help children become more confident and capable readers.

Materials provided by Texas A&M University. Original written by Ryan McCullar. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#746. JoBe Cerny, Actor, Director and Voice of the Pillsbury Doughboy, Dies at 78

The Second City alum also guided dozens of Hollywood stars in an expansive audio production of the Bible called ‘The Word of Promise.’

JoBe Cerny, who voiced the playful Pillsbury Doughboy in commercials and appeared in films including Somewhere in Time, My Best Friend’s Wedding and Road to Perdition, has died. He was 78.

Cerny lived in Grayslake, Illinois, and died Oct. 30, his family announced. He had battled Alzheimer’s disease.

For more than 30 years, Cerny owned and operated Cerny/American Creative Recording Studio in the River North neighborhood of Chicago. His company completed thousands of projects, including commercials, features and audiobooks. Related Stories TV Toukie Smith, Top Runway Model and '227' Actress, Dies at 74 Movies Donnie Dunagan, Original Voice of Bambi, Dies at 92

One of his finest accomplishments was directing a 98-hour dramatized audio production of the New King James Version of the Bible called The Word of Promise that featured more than 500 actors, among them Jim Caviezel as Jesus, Marisa Tomei as Mary Magdalene, Richard Dreyfuss as Moses, Gary Sinise as David, Jason Alexander as Joseph, Max von Sydow as Noah, Jon Voight as Abraham, Luke Perry as Judas and Marcia Gay Harden as Esther.

Cerny also converted episodes of CBS’ The Twilight Zone into radio programing and wrote new installments for a podcast series.

Cerny succeeded Paul Frees and Jeff Bergman as the high-pitched voice of the Pillsbury Co.’s cheerful Pillsbury Doughboy, who giggled when poked in the belly (he played the lovable Poppin’ Fresh character until about 2020).

“I’ve gone through phases over the years,” he said in a 2007 interview. “Sometimes [Pillsbury gets] a new executive. One guy said, ‘You know, I’ve always hated the voice of the Doughboy. And that’s you. I’m gonna do everything I can to not let the Doughboy talk anymore.’

“This was about seven years ago. That guy lost his job. He got fired the next year and a whole floor of people got fired with him. And then the next year I talked twice as much to make up for it.”

He also portrayed without dialogue “The Cheer Man” (also known as the “Silent Demonstrator”) in commercials for Procter & Gamble’s Cheer detergent; got killed “thousands of times” as bugs in Raid spots; and voiced a Scrubbing Bubble in spots for Dow Bathroom Cleaner.

Cerny was born on Dec 5, 1947, in Cicero, Illinois. His parents, Joe and Bea, combined their names for their son’s first name.

Cerny graduated from Morton East High School in Cicero in 1966, then earned his bachelor’s degree in Speech & Drama from Valparaiso University — he had planned to enter the seminary — and his master’s in Theater from Northwestern University.

In the 1970s, he joined The Second City to perform improv on its mainstage in Chicago and for its national touring company.

He played a desk clerk in Somewhere in Time (1980), a tailor in My Best Friend’s Wedding (1997) and a banker in Road to Perdition (2002).

The gregarious Cerny also showed up on the big screen in Rent-a-Cop (1987), Mo’ Money (1992), Love and Action in Chicago (1999), Novocaine (2001) and Legally Blonde 2: Red, White & Blonde (2003) and on episodes of Lady Blue, Early Edition and Chicago Hope.

Cerny wrote a weekly column for Screen Magazine called “ADventures in Advertising,” drove go-karts well into his 60s and was an enthusiastic model train collector.

Survivors include his wife of 56 years, Eileen; sons Tim and Patrick; daughters-in-law Andrea and Lily; and grandchildren Archer and Cleo.

“I’m lucky, I get to be somebody different every day, and in the end, I’m glad I stuck with my irresponsible decision to have fun,” he once said. “It allows me to live happily ever after … every day.”

#745. Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired

Why does the left side of the brain control the right side of the body, while the right side controls the left? This unusual arrangement is one of the most intriguing features of the nervous system, and scientists have proposed a new explanation that reaches back hundreds of millions of years.

Dr. Martin Wessendorf, a neuroscientist and associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota, studies how the brainstem regulates neurons in the spinal cord. Daniel Wang specializes in cognitive neuroscience and neurodegenerative diseases. Together, they have examined the evolutionary origins of the brain's crossed connections.

In a study published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, the researchers explore several neural circuits in four-limbed animals that are cross-wired (meaning one side of the brain connects with the opposite side of the body). Their hypothesis suggests that these connections may have developed because evolution built new brain circuits around an ancient visual system.

The brain contains numerous pathways that cross from one side of the central nervous system to the other. Understanding why these contralateral (midline-crossing) connections exist requires examining how different sensory and movement circuits developed over evolutionary time.

How the Brain Processes Visual Information

One possible explanation begins with the eyes. When light passes through the eye's lens, the image projected onto the retina is reversed. Objects appearing to our right are projected onto the left side of the retina, while objects on our left are projected onto the right.

Visual information travels along the optic nerve to a structure called the optic chiasm. Here, nerve fibers are organized so that information from the right visual field reaches the left side of the brain, while information from the left visual field is directed to the right side.

Some of these signals reach an ancient brain structure called the optic tectum (which in mammals is called the superior colliculus). Located in the midbrain, this region helps produce fast reactions to visual events, such as suddenly noticing something moving nearby.

Each side of the optic tectum contains a representation of the opposite visual field. Deeper within the structure, information about physical sensations (somatosensory information) is also organized into corresponding maps.

Because the optic tectum exists in every vertebrate species, it is considered one of the most ancient structures in the vertebrate nervous system. Its early appearance may be especially important for understanding why so many other neural pathways cross sides.

Why Sensory Signals Cross the Brain and Spinal Cord

The researchers also examined two major pathways responsible for transmitting sensations from the body to the brain. Both cross the center of the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord), and both appear to be widespread among tetrapods (the animals with four limbs, including mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians).

The first, called the dorsal column pathway, carries information about gentle touch, vibration, and the position of different body parts. Signals from the limbs and torso travel upward through the dorsal portion of the spinal cord before reaching another neuron in the brainstem, just above the spinal cord. From there, the pathway crosses to the opposite side.

Although fish lack this pathway, scientists have identified it in amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Its presence across these major animal groups suggests that the arrangement emerged early in tetrapod evolution and has remained largely conserved.

The second pathway, known as the spinothalamic tract, transmits sensations involving pain, itching, and certain types of touch. Unlike the dorsal column pathway, it crosses to the opposite side within the spinal cord itself.

After crossing, signals travel upward to the thalamus, a brain region located above the midbrain that plays a central role in processing sensory and movement information.

This crossed arrangement is found in birds, mammals, and reptiles. It also occurs in some cartilaginous fish, including sharks and rays, suggesting that aspects of this organization have even deeper evolutionary roots.

How the Brain Controls Movement Across the Body

The crossed organization of the nervous system extends beyond sensation. The researchers identified three important pathways involved in controlling skeletal muscles that also connect one side of the brain with the opposite side of the spinal cord.

The first is the tectospinal pathway, which helps the body respond rapidly to information from the environment.

The optic tectum processes more than vision. It also receives information about sounds and physical sensations, organizing these signals into maps that align with its visual representation on the opposite side of the brain.

Imagine preparing to cross a street when you suddenly notice a car approaching from the corner of your eye. You instinctively turn toward the vehicle. The tectospinal pathway is one of the neural circuits that helps produce this rapid response. It can also coordinate similar reactions to unexpected sounds or touch.

The movement signals originate in the deepest layers of the optic tectum and travel through nerve fibers to the opposite side of the spinal cord. This pathway is present in most tetrapods and certain cartilaginous fish.

Another important circuit is the rubrospinal pathway, which is thought to help animals control their limbs. It begins in a midbrain structure called the red nucleus and extends to the opposite side of the spinal cord. The pathway is especially prominent in most mammals, although it has also been identified in other tetrapods and some cartilaginous fish.

The Evolution of Fine Motor Control in Humans

The third pathway, called the corticospinal tract, has a particularly important role in humans because it supports precise movements, including the fine control of our fingers.

Its evolutionary history is more complicated than that of the other pathways.

All vertebrates possess a telencephalon, the forward portion of the brain that accounts for much of the brain's overall size in humans. However, only mammals have a cerebral cortex organized into six distinct layers.

This six-layered cortex supports sophisticated functions such as combining sensory information with memories, coordinating movement, and processing language.

The corticospinal pathway extends from the cerebral cortex toward the spinal cord, but its function varies among animals.

In most mammals, it primarily influences sensory processing. Nerve fibers reach spinal cord regions that receive information from the body, allowing the brain to regulate incoming sensations.

In primates (including humans) and certain other animals capable of highly precise movements, the pathway also reaches spinal cord regions responsible for controlling muscles. These connections make intricate actions possible, including the coordinated finger movements needed for delicate tasks.

Depending on the species, the corticospinal tract can regulate sensory information or contribute directly to movement. In either case, its fibers cross the midline of the nervous system.

The researchers suggest that humans may have developed advanced fine motor abilities by adapting an older neural circuit originally involved in controlling sensory input. Rather than creating an entirely new system, evolution may have given an existing pathway an additional purpose.

A 500-Million-Year-Old Explanation for the Brain's Crossed Wiring

Taken together, these neural pathways point toward a potentially surprising explanation for the brain's unusual organization.

The researchers propose that the earliest visual circuits helped establish a pattern in which sensory and movement pathways were organized across opposite sides of the nervous system. Later circuits may have inherited this arrangement as they evolved, particularly in tetrapods.

Because every living vertebrate possesses an optic chiasm and an optic tectum organized around information from the opposite visual field, the researchers suspect that these structures were already present in primitive jawless fish during the Cambrian Period, approximately 538 to 486 million years ago.

If correct, this would mean that the basic organization underlying the brain's crossed connections began developing more than half a billion years before modern humans appeared.

The hypothesis may even be testable. Scientists could examine fossilized skulls from ancient jawless fish for anatomical evidence that might help establish whether these early animals possessed an optic chiasm and optic tectum.

An Evolutionary Inheritance Rather Than an Advantage?

The broader idea challenges the assumption that every unusual biological feature must have evolved because it provided a direct survival benefit.

Evolution often modifies structures that already exist instead of developing completely new systems. Once the ancient visual pathways established a crossed organization, that arrangement may have influenced how additional sensory and motor circuits developed.

In particular, the organization of the visual system (and in particular, the optic tectum) may have provided a structural foundation that later pathways followed.

Under this hypothesis, the brain's crossed connections did not necessarily arise because controlling the opposite side of the body was inherently more effective. Instead, they may reflect the lasting influence of an ancient arrangement that evolution repeatedly reused.

The result could be one of the most enduring examples of how the nervous system preserves its evolutionary history. The strange relationship between the brain's two hemispheres and the opposite sides of the body may ultimately trace back to the visual systems of animals that lived more than 500 million years ago.

Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#744. How David Leitch Made ‘How to Rob a Bank’ on a Budget — and Around Nicholas Hoult’s Torn ACL

The action filmmaker moved fast — and got creative — to shoot the movie in half the days of his previous movie, 'The Fall Guy,' all with an injured leading man.

Director David Leitch has spent his career designing high-octane action for audiences to enjoy on the big screen. How to Rob a Bank, his sixth feature film since co-directing John Wick, is the first he’s made to inspire audiences to take action themselves.

At a certain point in How to Rob a Bank, the fourth wall is broken to deliver a shot across the bow to those in power: Either fix the broken economic system, or we’ll fix it for you. Nov. 3rd’s midterm elections were Americans’ way of pursuing the latter and taking matters into their own hands by electing candidates who prioritized combating the rising cost of living. Related Stories TV Nicholas Hoult Boards 'Harry Potter' Season 2 as Gilderoy Lockhart Movies 'Jason Statham Stole My Bike': David Leitch's Action-Comedy Sets Summer 2027 Release

When The Hollywood Reporter caught up with Leitch last month ahead of the midterms, the filmmaker remained optimistic that economic policies, both macro and micro, could still be corrected, starting at the ballot box.

“How to Rob a Bank challenges individuals to change the system. [Our protagonists] are asking you to be proactive in the ways that you can. Go out and vote for what you believe in. We still live in a democracy,” Leitch told The Hollywood Reporter on Oct. 5 in support of How to Rob a Bank’s Nov. 13 theatrical release. “I hope How to Rob a Bank is empowering and inspiring to people.”

The heist dramedy follows a crew of altruistic bank robbers who document their exploits on social media, hoping to galvanize others who share their belief that the American Dream has been hijacked by predatory, merciless institutions.

Led by Nicholas Hoult’s charismatic “The Wolf,” the masked gang behind the wildly popular YouTube channel Who’s Hungry? soon finds itself in the crosshairs of a frustrated FBI agent (John C. Reilly) and his newest ace in the hole, a criminal programmer (Zoë Kravitz) who agrees to help unmask the Robin Hood-esque thieves in exchange for her release from house arrest.

Considering that the film is produced and distributed by Amazon MGM, it’s worth noting that its parent company, the world’s largest by revenue, made no attempt to temper the film’s late-stage anti-capitalist stance.

“The filmmaking core at Amazon MGM are just trying to make great films that have all different types of messages,” Leitch says. “They want things to be provocative, and they want to encourage artists to speak their mind. So there was never any pushback from the studio about what we were making.”

For a film that wasn’t originally scripted to take place in the blue-collar city of Pittsburgh, it became the most Pittsburgh movie since The Dark Knight Rises, only more so since it shot Pittsburgh for Pittsburgh, not Gotham City. The production reportedly poured nearly $60 million into the Steel City’s local economy to qualify for a tax incentive. Still, Leitch describes the film as a relatively modest undertaking compared to his previous feature, The Fall Guy, which carried an estimated budget of $125 million to $150 million.

“We shot this in 40 days, and just to give you context, The Fall Guy was 86 days. So How to Rob a Bank is half the size of that film, and we just had to move quicker,” Leitch shares.

To make the most of those limited shooting days, Leitch deployed a second unit he dubbed the “YouTube unit,” made up primarily of stunt performers tasked with capturing the masked robbery sequences. This allowed Leitch and his ensemble — Hoult, Kravitz, Anna Sawai, Pete Davidson, Rhenzy Feliz, Reilly, and Christian Slater — to concentrate on the characters’ personal lives and the surprisingly dramatic territory the film gradually explores.

To distinguish the world of the anonymous YouTube characters from the real lives of the people behind them, Leitch and his team shot the in-universe videos on prosumer digital cameras, while the unmasked drama was filmed on 35mm film. Given the original film’s mid-budget constraints, Leitch acknowledges that the celluloid format required “a lot of number crunching.”

The second unit of masked stunt performers also proved particularly valuable in light of Hoult’s major injury at the time. Shortly before production began, the English actor tore his ACL while playing basketball. Rather than undergo surgery and drop out of the pic, he committed to intensive physical therapy three times a week to prepare for the demands of How to Rob a Bank. Leitch and his producing partner/wife, Kelly McCormick, nevertheless spared him considerable physical pain by structuring the shoot as they did.

But working around bad knees is old hat for Leitch, thanks to his background in the stunt department. Even Keanu Reeves dealt with a bum knee on the first John Wick — and, for that matter, throughout much of the franchise.

Below, during a conversation with THR, Leitch also discusses his next film, Jason Statham Stole My Bike, starring, you guessed it, Jason Statham.

Since John Wick, you’ve shot seven films, but you’ve been attached to at least a dozen more movies in development. How did How to Rob a Bank overtake everything else you’ve been juggling?

I love to find action genres and put my own spin on them and turn them on their head. I got to do it in the superhero genre with Deadpool 2. I got to do it in Atomic Blonde where we took a noir and made it a neon noir. I also got to do a romantic comedy with The Fall Guy. But I hadn’t done a heist movie. And when we read the script for How to Rob a Bank, I got really excited about how contemporary it was. It had this social media component, this content creator idea, that was so strong and interesting. Then it had these really grounded characters who were dealing with very timely issues that a lot of people are dealing with right now. So it just felt undeniable, and it moved to the top of the list very quickly.

How to Rob a Bank is a David-versus-Goliath story with an anti-capitalist message, and yet it’s being distributed by Amazon, the largest company in the world by annual revenue. Did they ever acknowledge that irony in your meetings together?

No, the filmmaking core at Amazon MGM are just trying to make great films with good filmmakers and that have all different types of messages. They want things to be provocative, and they want to encourage artists to speak their mind. So there was never any pushback from the studio about what we were making.

The original draft by Mark Bianculli wasn’t fully what you saw at the end of this film. The content creator aspect was more inspired by me and how I felt these characters would really make a show. It was really a nuts-and-bolts how-to in the script, and I was like, These people have an agenda and would need a personal message. They would need to be more evangelical to bring these followers in.

So I put it through that prism of, What’s the message they are really telling? And they started to tell this message about the inequalities that are happening and the systems that aren’t working for them in an edutainment kind of way. The Wolf is having fun while educating you on his worldview.

We still made a movie with characters that are on both sides, and at the end of the day, I just want the audience to make their own decision of how they want to enact change. I certainly do not want them to rob banks, but they can be proactive in a lot of different ways if they choose to be.

The movie demands those in power to fix the broken system. Do you think it’s even salvageable? Is it broken beyond repair?

That’s a good question, and I don’t have the answer to it. I hope it’s not [broken beyond repair]. But I do think How to Rob a Bank challenges individuals to change the system. It doesn’t necessarily challenge the people in power to change the system. At the end of the movie, our protagonists, if you want to call them that, took on something that was extremely radical. But what they’re asking you to do is be proactive in the ways that you can: help your friend, give back, find a charity to work for. There are other ways to change your community. Go out and vote for what you believe in. You can change the systems. We still live in a democracy.

But that being said, it does feel hard. It’s daunting. There’s a big power [imbalance], and the movie expresses a lot of that frustration. Can it be changed? I hope so. I hope it’s empowering and inspiring to people. Get out there and try to do something about it.

Instead of auditioning, did Nicholas Hoult just send you a copy of his recent movie The Order in which he plays a bankrobber?

(Laughs.) First of all, Nick didn’t have to audition. We’ve been circling projects for years. I think Nick is one of the great actors of his generation, and he’s now coming into his own. He really responded to the contemporary material as much as Kelly [McCormick] and I did. It had something to say, and we knew we could lean into that in a fun way. So I can’t say enough about Nick.

His first day on set, he didn’t really understand how I was going to create this content creator world. He got to set late after we’d already been shooting for a week, and dressed as the Wolf in a security guard outfit, he had to deliver this whole monologue about the security guards’ struggles to make ends meet. And he was like, “Wait, what movie am I in right now?” (Laughs.) But he took it all in stride and really embraced the charismatic nature that this guy had to have to create such a successful YouTube show.

Nick had a tough go of it on this movie. He basically had to shoot it on one leg.

Did the wolf mask come in handy considering he had a torn ACL?

The mask actually helped us in a lot of ways. We did this movie at a lower price point. It was a little smaller budget, and that’s partly because you have to make original content for a price. That’s how the economics of film work.

So we had the heist crew, played by stunt performers, out there shooting the [YouTube robbery] stuff on prosumer cameras, including DJI drones and Insta360s. We did that as second unit with stunt people because they were all in the masks, and we could create a lot of footage for the social media content. I could then really focus on the drama with Pete [Davidson], John [C. Reilly], Zoe [Kravitz], Nick, Anna [Sawai], Rhenzy [Feliz]. That’s the other half of the film, and it’s shot in a very different way. So the masks helped.

When Nick’s character is limping in the street, was that his real limp? Or did he embellish it since the character had been beaten up at that point?

He was leaning into it. He was embellishing it. He was embracing the beating that he took in the garage and pulling his character together. It wasn’t an extension of reality.

Keanu had a bad knee on the first Wick, though not torn-ACL-level bad. It’s actually been a recurring issue on all of them. In any event, you’ve probably got a playbook for this sort of thing, right?

Yeah, I do. There’s a lot of ways to shoot action, and there’s a lot of movie magic that can happen in that space. It’s all about how you choose to choreograph something and how you choose to capture it. Fortunately, Keanu is another person who’s probably the toughest human being on the planet. He just powered through it. We were able to film those sequences with him really doing the action, and the first Wick was 99 percent Keanu.

With Nick and How to Rob a Bank, there’s not as much action, but there is that fight scene in the garage. It was probably his biggest physical set piece, and it was mostly him, barring a crash into a window where someone could get really hurt.

You mentioned that you shot this movie for a price, but you still managed to capture the real-life drama on 35mm film and the Who’s Hungry? social media material on digital. How much arm twisting did you have to do to pull off a dual format?

It was a lot of number crunching, as you always have to do. No matter what size budget, there’s always number crunching, and it usually ultimately comes down to days. We shot this in 40 days, and just to give you context, The Fall Guy was 86 days. So How to Rob a Bank is half the size of that film, and we just had to move quicker. There was a little more planning involved, and we chose a style that required less coverage. So all those things were put through the prism of making a film of this size.

It’s expensive to shoot on film because we generally no longer shoot on film. It’s kind of a bespoke process, so there’s less people doing it, and it’s just more expensive. It’s a bummer because it’s a great format with such a beautiful aesthetic, and it just reacts to light so much differently. I grew up shooting film as a second unit director, and it was right around the time I started directing on the first Wick where digital just basically took over. So it has always been a financial matter, but it was really fun to go back to it.

Early on, Zoe’s character speaks on behalf of her guinea pig named Morpheus. Was she upset that you dubbed over her voice with your own voice?

(Laughs.) She was not upset because she didn’t know about it. During the mix, we were limited in terms of time. We were running out of mix days. So Mark Stoeckinger, who’s a great sound designer that I’ve worked with since Wick, was like, “We need something for the guinea pig. Just get on the mic. Let’s go.” So he put my voice through his beautiful machine, and next thing you know, that’s my cameo.

Zoe is in for a big surprise at the premiere.

The John Wick documentary, Wick is Pain, revealed that the Wick choreography was originally intended for Jason Statham in Safe, but the final product only has a small trace of it.

You are now in post on a movie called Jason Statham Stole My Bike. Is this Jason’s way of saying he regrets not utilizing that style way back when?

(Laughs.) I don’t think it’s his way of saying that. Jason and I have had a longtime friendship. We go way back to my time as a fight choreographer and a stunt performer on Ghosts of Mars. He was the third lead in that film. I did some stunts for him on that, and then we did a lot of choreography together in other films along the way. So we’ve offered up a lot of different styles for him, but he’s made his own brand. It’s been working pretty well for him, so he’s going to be okay.

Is this movie even more meta than The Fall Guy?

It’s its own thing. It’s very different from The Fall Guy. The meta of The Fall Guy was really reflective of the industry, and it was ultimately a romcom surrounded by a meta action film. Jason Statham Stole My Bike is as unique as the title itself, and it is an entertaining ride that’s going to hopefully be a fun four-quadrant film with a lot of twists and turns that people aren’t going to expect.

The last four movies of yours, counting Statham, have been original or semi-original. The Fall Guy and Bullet Train were based on existing works, but they’re first-time adaptations on the big screen. It seems to me like you’re happier in this realm, but are you still open to franchises if they come your way?

I’m open to all of it. I also did a lot of franchises as a second unit director. I spent a lot of time working in a world to amplify a director’s vision or even support studio notes inside of a big franchise. I would shoot that stuff as a second unit director.

But as an artist, I love original material. I love to be allowed to create the world and set the aesthetic — and not have the expectation of what the IP brings to it. It just allows you to have a truer voice of who you are as an artist, so I appreciate you thinking about that.

Original material is harder to get funded, though. It just is. That’s again why we had to do How to Rob a Bank for a smaller price. And Jason Statham Stole My Bike is even smaller in the sense that it’s such a bold idea. But it doesn’t bother me. It’s a problem-opportunity. So, at the end of the day, it’s more fun for me to be original.

***How to Rob a Bank opens in theaters Nov. 13.

#743. Black Lives Matter Activist DeRay Mckesson Talks Losing Key Trump-Era Protest Mobilization Tool: “I Miss Twitter”

The ‘Pod Save the People’ co-host was discussing street-level protests versus policy advocacy with 'The Hollywood Reporter' editor-in-chief Maer Roshan while at Web Summit 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal.

Activist DeRay Mckesson, while today a podcaster and digital storyteller, in 2014 first made a name for himself as a street-level Black Lives Matter protester and a leading voice against police violence.

So Mckesson has a unique perspective as both a social issues activist at the street level and behind a microphone and in front of a camera. And on Tuesday at the Web Summit in Lisbon, he pointed with nostalgia to a once-powerful protest mobilization tool no longer at hand.

“I miss Twitter. Twitter rest in peace. It was such a powerful platform for us back then,” Mckesson, an executive director of Campaign Zero, argued during a session entitled From Chaos to the Campaign moderated by Maer Roshan, editor-in-chief of The Hollywood Reporter and also webcast. Related Stories Business The Hollywood Reporter Launches Turkish Edition General News Trump Reflects on Republicans' Midterm Losses, Reacts to J.D. Vance's Own Analysis in '60 Minutes' Interview

Roshan, who was part of ACT UP, a 1980s group that redefined social activism, and McKesson discussed whether chaotic street protests or strategic policy work were more effective drivers of political change.

In response, McKesson praised the subversive utility of Twitter and Vine to get protesters onto the street. Of course, that’s before Donald Trump was first elected U.S. president, Elon Musk rebranded Twitter as X and slower-paced content from Instagram and TikTok increasingly came to dominate the social media space.

He added Instagram and TikTok had changed digital storytelling by getting civil rights activists away from tweeting in real time for rapid mobilization to taking longer and being more polished with content they distribute across social media platforms. “Especially on Instagram, capturing video footage and getting it out takes time,” Mckesson argued.

At the same time, the recent U.S. midterm elections underlined how civil rights campaigners today use Instagram and TikTok more widely and effectively to talk about candidates and competing stances on hot-button issues. “There are way more people with access to stories and sort of talking because of Instagram and TikTok, in a way that does feel different,” Mckesson insisted.

Elsewhere, he pointed to New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani as a social media master using an influencer operation to get the issue of affordability top-of-mind among New Yorkers when he first ran for political office. And ten years after Trump got to the White House, Mckesson argued social justice content creators enjoy greater traction as Americans increasingly tired of the U.S. president.

“ICE was a big part of the backlash to Trump,” he said of dramatic protests after hooded immigration enforcement agents made arrests at school graduations and birthday parties and attempted deportations across America.

Mckesson said opposition to ICE agent protests more easily cut through and were amplified compared to a decade ago: “In 2014-15, we were a small group of people worried about ICE. Now there’s huge groups of people who don’t even identify as protesters or activists and are pushing on ICE. There are reporters questioning jail deaths in a way that just wasn’t happening.”

And mainstream media is today more likely to cover and raise the alarm on social and political issues and enable calls to grassroots change. “We do see legacy media sort of helping us challenge systems when some of the stuff is just so bizarre, but people think that’s normal,” Mckesson told the Web Summit informal conversation.

Today, he is also co-host of the Pod Save the People podcast from Crooked Media that explores social justice, culture and politics via a platform a long ways from street-level protests during the Black Lives Matter movement. Mckesson insists he’s fine advocating to the converted when it comes to supporting people of color and representing underrepresented voices calling for meaningful change.

“I’m okay with preaching to the choir. The choir needs good messaging. I do think people are smarter today than they were in 2014. People can handle nuanced conversation in a way that is actually really powerful,” he said.

#742. A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests

Something unusual is happening inside the enormous atmosphere of Betelgeuse, one of the most recognizable stars in the night sky. Astronomers have detected subtle changes in the star's shape that suggest something is moving through its outer layers, disturbing the surrounding gas like an unseen visitor making noise inside a house. (Metaphorically speaking.) New observations point to a likely culprit: Siwarha, a recently discovered companion star that appears to be traveling through Betelgeuse's atmosphere.

Betelgeuse is a massive red supergiant located in the constellation Orion, where it forms the famous hunter's shoulder. Although the star has fascinated astronomers for generations, it attracted worldwide attention in late 2019 and early 2020 when its brightness unexpectedly plunged to its lowest recorded level in more than 100 years. The event, known as the Great Dimming, raised questions about what was happening inside the aging star.

Now, observations from the U.S. National Science Foundation's Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (NSF VLA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) reveal that Betelgeuse's vast outer atmosphere has largely returned to normal. More intriguingly, the measurements provide new evidence that a nearby companion star is physically disturbing the giant star's atmosphere.

The research was led by Dr. Lynn D. Matthews, Principal Research Scientist and Assistant Director at MIT Haystack Observatory, working with scientists from the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, the University of Manchester, and the European Southern Observatory. The team analyzed observations gathered between 2021 and 2026 at seven radio frequencies ranging from 22 GHz to 485 GHz.

Different radio frequencies allow astronomers to examine different depths within a star's atmosphere. By combining the observations from both telescopes, the researchers reconstructed the structure of Betelgeuse's outer layers, beginning just above its visible surface and extending outward to several times its radius.

"It was the combination of the incredible data from the NSF VLA and ALMA that gave us a convincing result here," said Matthews. "The fact that we can use these facilities to actually resolve the disks of nearby stars is amazing."

Betelgeuse Recovers From Its Mysterious Great Dimming

The latest measurements also help scientists understand how Betelgeuse has changed since its extraordinary fading episode. Several months before the Great Dimming (when Betelgeuse ejected a billion tons of solar material, partially blocking our view), an earlier investigation led by Matthews detected unusually low temperatures in the star's atmosphere at radio wavelengths.

At the time, researchers suggested that turbulent convection deep inside Betelgeuse may have generated a shock wave that traveled outward and disrupted the surrounding gas. That disturbance could have helped trigger the enormous release of material that later formed dust and obscured part of the star's light.

The new observations indicate that the atmosphere has since warmed to temperatures more typical of Betelgeuse. At a distance of approximately 2.7 times the star's radius, the gas now has a measured brightness temperature of about 3,500 Kelvin (comparable to Betelgeuse's own surface temperature).

Astronomers Discover an Unexpectedly Cold Atmospheric Layer

The researchers also confirmed a feature that scientists had suspected existed for years: a region of unusually cool gas between Betelgeuse's visible surface and its higher atmospheric layer, known as the chromosphere.

Using ALMA at its highest observed frequencies, the team was able to probe closer to the star's surface than previous radio measurements had allowed. The results revealed temperatures falling to approximately 2,200 Kelvin, more than 1,000 degrees below the temperature of the visible surface, or photosphere.

This cool region corresponds to the "MOLsphere," a layer containing molecular gas that astronomers had previously identified primarily through infrared observations. The new radio measurements provide a much more direct examination of this elusive part of Betelgeuse's atmosphere and confirm the long-suspected "temperature minimum."

A Hidden Companion Star May Be Distorting Betelgeuse

One of the most intriguing discoveries involves Siwarha, the smaller star believed to orbit extremely close to Betelgeuse. Astronomers first proposed the companion's existence in 2024 as a possible explanation for a puzzling cycle in which Betelgeuse's brightness changes approximately every 2,100 days. Subsequent direct imaging and spectroscopic observations have provided additional support for the companion's existence.

The name Siwarha reflects its relationship with Betelgeuse. The giant star's name comes from the Arabic expression meaning "the hand of al-Jawza," while Siwarha means "her bracelet."

Unlike a planet or star traveling far from its host, Siwarha is believed to follow an orbit that takes it directly through Betelgeuse's extended atmosphere. Its estimated orbital distance is only about twice the red supergiant's radius.

"This companion is orbiting so close to the star that it actually passes through its extended atmosphere," Matthews explained.

As Siwarha moves along its orbit, it may push through the surrounding gas much like a fast boat cutting through water. The resulting wake could disturb the atmosphere, producing changes that astronomers can detect even though the smaller star itself remains invisible in the radio observations.

In fact, the researchers calculated that Siwarha is likely tens to hundreds of times too faint to be detected directly with the radio measurements they collected. Instead, they searched for indirect evidence of its presence by studying the shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere.

Betelgeuse's Changing Shape Reveals New Clues

The scientists discovered that Betelgeuse does not always appear perfectly round at radio wavelengths. Its atmosphere sometimes develops a slightly stretched, oval appearance, and the timing of these changes appears to match the expected position of Siwarha.

To investigate this connection, the team measured the atmosphere's departure from a circular shape ("ellipticity") across observations taken at different times.

They found that Betelgeuse tends to look more elongated when Siwarha is expected to be at its greatest apparent separation from the giant star. When the companion is predicted to pass in front of or behind Betelgeuse from our perspective, the atmosphere appears rounder.

This relationship provides compelling evidence that the smaller star may be influencing the shape of Betelgeuse's outer layers through gravity and its physical passage through the gas.

The effect resembles noticing ripples spreading across a pond without being able to see what caused them. Although Siwarha remains too faint to identify directly at radio wavelengths, the changing shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere may reveal its movement around the larger star.

Future Observations Could Reveal More About Betelgeuse

Despite the promising results, astronomers emphasize that additional observations are necessary to confirm the connection between Siwarha's orbit and the atmospheric distortions. Measurements covering more of the companion's orbital cycle, particularly at radio frequencies that have not yet been studied extensively, could help establish how strongly the smaller star affects Betelgeuse.

More advanced instruments may eventually provide an even clearer picture. The Next Generation Very Large Array, an observatory currently under development, is expected to make detailed studies of nearby stars and their atmospheres much easier.

Such observations could reveal not only how companion stars influence their massive neighbors, but also how aging red supergiants lose material as they approach the final stages of their lives. Understanding these interactions may help astronomers better explain the complicated processes that shape the evolution of enormous stars like Betelgeuse.

The findings were published in The Astronomical Journal in a paper titled "New Spatially Resolved Observations of Betelgeuse from the VLA and ALMA: Evidence for Atmospheric Perturbations from a Close Companion."
